areas.name: Matrix analysis toolkit
areas.summary: Deterministic facts every RandNLA proof reaches for: SVD, best low-rank approximation, perturbation, projections, pseudoinverse, trace inequalities, the Loewner order.

areas.name: Trace inequalities and the Loewner order
Random matrices
areas.summary: Matrix-valued random models: Gaussian laws and inverse moments, spectral bounds, covariance, matrix chaos, Gaussian comparison and spectral universality.

areas.name: Extreme eigenvalues, singular values and covariance
areas.summary: Spectral norm, extreme eigenvalue and singular-value estimates, including lower bounds for sample covariance matrices.

areas.name: Probability and concentration
areas.summary: Scalar and matrix probability bounds, Gaussian and exchangeable-pair identities, moment-generating functions, independence and martingales. Deterministic matrix-function theory lives under Matrix.

areas.name: Sketching primitives
areas.summary: Johnson–Lindenstrauss, subspace embeddings, approximate matrix multiplication, leverage-score sampling. The vocabulary in which randomized algorithms are analysed.

areas.name: Leverage scores, volume sampling and determinantal laws
areas.summary: Importance sampling, leverage scores, determinant-weighted subsets, L-ensembles and their exact sampling and moment identities.

areas.name: Low-rank approximation
areas.summary: Deterministic structural lemmas (projection error, truncation, power iteration, Nyström) and the randomized algorithm guarantees that consume them.

areas.name: Trace, diagonal and spectral estimation
areas.summary: Trace, diagonal and quadratic-form estimators, residual certificates, and spectral-density reconstruction from randomized Krylov or Chebyshev moments.

areas.name: Krylov and iterative methods
areas.summary: Stationary linear iterations, Krylov subspaces, Lanczos, conjugate gradient, Gauss quadrature and the spectral measure: deterministic theory resting on the matrix and polynomial layers. Randomized Krylov guarantees (random-start Lanczos, block Krylov, SLQ) sit with their consumers in low-rank approximation and estimation.

areas.name: Randomized solvers (consumers)
areas.summary: Sketch-and-solve, sketch-and-precondition, Kaczmarz and sketch-and-project. Mostly consumers of sketching and matrix facts; Kaczmarz is itself a clean foundation.

areas.name: Gaussian measure: log-Sobolev and comparison
areas.summary: Gaussian-vector geometry and the machinery behind Gaussian concentration and Gordon's theorem: Gaussian width, integration by parts, the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck semigroup, log-Sobolev, Herbst, Slepian and Sudakov–Fernique.

areas.name: Polynomial approximation
areas.summary: Chebyshev polynomials and their extremal properties, Markov-type derivative bounds, interpolation. Layer 0, no matrices: the deterministic polynomial facts that Krylov, Lanczos, CG and block Krylov rates reduce to.

areas.name: Chebyshev polynomials
areas.summary: Growth outside [-1,1], second kind, extremal and minimax properties, monic minimality.

areas.name: Approximation, derivatives, interpolation
areas.summary: Gap-amplifying polynomials, approximation of 1/x, Markov and Bernstein inequalities, Lagrange remainder and Chebyshev interpolation.

areas.name: Krylov bases: grade, Arnoldi and Lanczos relations
areas.title: Krylov bases: grade, Arnoldi and Lanczos relations
areas.summary: Dimension of Krylov spaces, the Arnoldi relation and its Hessenberg matrix, exactness of Krylov projection on polynomials, block Krylov spaces.

areas.name: Iterative methods for linear systems
areas.title: Iterative methods for linear systems
areas.summary: Stationary and regular splittings, Richardson and Chebyshev iteration, residual polynomials, GMRES, MINRES, FOM, preconditioned CG and CGLS/LSQR, with their convergence certificates and spectral bounds.

areas.name: Field of values and non-normal GMRES theory
areas.title: Field of values and non-normal GMRES theory
areas.summary: Numerical range, Crouzeix–Palencia, the Elman / Beckermann–Goreinov–Tyrtyshnikov bounds and the Greenbaum–Pták–Strakoš caution.

areas.name: Krylov approximation of f(A)b
areas.title: Krylov approximation of f(A)b
areas.summary: Lanczos-FA and Arnoldi-FA: the Krylov approximation of a matrix function times a vector is within twice (Hermitian) or 2(1+√2) times (general) the best polynomial approximation error.

areas.name: Ritz values and eigenvector angles
areas.title: Ritz values and eigenvector angles
areas.summary: Gap-dependent Kaniel–Paige–Saad theory: the angle between an eigenvector and the Krylov space, and the Ritz value error.

areas.name: Chebyshev series and analytic approximation
areas.title: Chebyshev series and analytic approximation
areas.summary: Chebyshev coefficients, Bernstein ellipses, aliasing, and the ATAP convergence theorems (3.1, 4.1–4.2, 7.1–7.2, 8.1–8.2).

areas.name: Best approximation, Jackson and Lebesgue constants
areas.title: Best approximation, Jackson and Lebesgue constants
areas.summary: E_n(f), equioscillation and de la Vallée Poussin, Jackson's theorem, Lebesgue constants of interpolation.

areas.name: Approximating specific functions, with lower bounds
areas.title: Approximating specific functions, with lower bounds
areas.summary: x^s, e^{-x}, x^{-1/2}, log x, sign(x) with explicit degrees, and the matching degree lower bounds (1/x, e^{-x}, sign).

areas.name: Majorization, Ky Fan and unitarily invariant norms
areas.title: Majorization, Ky Fan and unitarily invariant norms
areas.summary: Majorization of spectra, Ky Fan / Schatten / unitarily invariant norms, and the eigenvalue and singular-value inequalities stated with them (Ky Fan, Schur–Horn, Lidskii, Horn).

areas.name: Subspace angles and sin θ theorems
areas.title: Subspace angles and sin θ theorems
areas.summary: Canonical angles between subspaces and the Davis–Kahan / Wedin perturbation bounds for eigen- and singular subspaces.

areas.name: Linear systems, inverses and conditioning
areas.title: Linear systems, inverses and conditioning
areas.summary: Inverse perturbation and condition numbers, forward-error bounds for linear systems and least squares, and reduced-Hessian solvability of constrained systems.

areas.name: Orthogonal polynomials, Jacobi matrices and Gauss-type quadrature
areas.title: Orthogonal polynomials, Jacobi matrices and Gauss-type quadrature
areas.summary: Orthogonal polynomials of a measure (general and spectral), zeros and interlacing, Christoffel numbers, Gauss, Radau and Lobatto rules and their remainders, kernel polynomials and modifications, moments and the modified Chebyshev algorithm (Gautschi 2004).

areas.name: Residual certification and adaptive validation
areas.summary: Independent tests of residual operators, conditional guarantees, and valid error budgets for adaptive stopping.

areas.name: Laplacians, resistance and spectral approximation
areas.summary: Incidence, nullspaces and pseudoinverses connect graph quadratic forms to matrix approximation and leverage sampling.

areas.name: Least squares, regularization and matrix nearness
areas.summary: Ordinary and total least squares, spectral regularization and filtered pseudoinverses, and nearest positive-semidefinite matrices.

areas.name: Displacement structure and rational low-rank approximation
areas.summary: Sylvester displacement rank, rational rank identities, and Zolotarev singular-value decay.

areas.name: Singular-value shrinkage and matrix penalties
areas.summary: SVD-based shrinkage primitives and exact minimization for nuclear-norm and rank penalties.

areas.name: Projection methods for matrix equations
areas.summary: Galerkin projections for Sylvester, Lyapunov, and multiterm matrix operators.

areas.name: Projection costs and deterministic covariance sketches
areas.summary: Projection-cost preservation and deterministic shrinkage certificates, connecting sketches to low-rank optimization.

areas.name: Regularized sketches and effective dimension
areas.summary: Ridge leverage scores, effective dimension, regularized spectral approximation and determinantal sampling.

areas.name: Matrix functions, positive maps and matrix means
areas.summary: Functional calculus, Fréchet derivatives and divided differences, positive maps and matrix means, sign and polar iterations, and trace-exponential representations.

areas.name: Matrix chaos and covariance-sensitive bounds
areas.summary: Decoupling, coefficient-tensor flattenings and matrix polynomial moments; Gaussian bounds using full entry covariance.

areas.name: Sylvester, Lyapunov and Stein equations
areas.summary: Solvability, separation, stability and residuals of finite matrix equations, with ADI and doubling recurrences. Projection methods remain under Krylov.

areas.name: Gaussian comparison, free models and spectral laws
areas.summary: Gaussian proxies with matching covariance, spectral comparisons with free models, resolvent-trace universality, and variational formulas for limiting matrix spectra.

areas.name: Nonnegative matrices and M-matrices
areas.summary: Perron–Frobenius theory, Collatz–Wielandt certificates, primitive power limits, inverse positivity and elimination for nonsingular M-matrices. Positivity in this area is entrywise, rather than the Loewner order.

areas.name: Fourier methods and structured matrix computation
areas.summary: Fourier diagonalization, circulant solves and pseudoinverses, exact FFT realizations and Toeplitz products through circulant embeddings.

areas.name: Dynamic mode decomposition, realization and model reduction
areas.summary: Finite snapshot operators, exact Hankel realization, Gramian balancing and empirical interpolation.

areas.name: Hierarchical matrices and structured direct solvers
areas.summary: HODLR and nested HSS/HBS representations, explicit storage and matvec models, compression certificates and inverse rank structure.

areas.name: Spectral density and robust moment reconstruction
areas.summary: Probability measures on matrix spectra, noisy Chebyshev moments, positive kernel reconstruction, and Hermitian or normal matrix query algorithms.

areas.name: Structured random matrices
areas.summary: Finite-group Fourier blocks and structured Gaussian ensembles.

areas.name: Real stability, interlacing and finite free convolution
areas.summary: Finite polynomial methods for matrix spectra: common interlacing, mixed characteristic polynomials and finite free convolutions.

areas.name: Spectral selection, partitions and sparsification
areas.summary: Deterministic spectral existence theorems: sparse identity decompositions, frame partitions and quantitatively invertible column subsets.

results.title: Frobenius and spectral norms: mixed inequalities
results.informal: Submultiplicativity: $\|AB\|_F \le \|A\|\,\|B\|_F$ and $\|AB\|_F \le \|A\|_F\,\|B\|$. Norm comparison: $\|A\| \le \|A\|_F \le \sqrt{\operatorname{rank}(A)}\,\|A\|$. Both norms are unitarily invariant, and $$\|A\|_F^2 = \operatorname{tr}(A^\top A) = \sum_i \sigma_i^2.$$
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$
$B \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$
results.conclusion: $\|AB\|_F \le \|A\|\,\|B\|_F$, $\|AB\|_F \le \|A\|_F\,\|B\|$, $\|A\| \le \|A\|_F \le \sqrt{\operatorname{rank}(A)}\,\|A\|$ and $\|A\|_F^2 = \operatorname{tr}(A^\top A) = \sum_i \sigma_i^2$

results.title: Singular value decomposition of a matrix
results.informal: Every $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ factors as $A = U\Sigma V^\top$ with $U, V$ orthogonal and $\Sigma$ diagonal with $\sigma_1 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_{\min(m,n)} \ge 0$. Splitting at rank $k$ gives the block form $$A = U_1\Sigma_1V_1^\top + U_2\Sigma_2V_2^\top.$$
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$
split index $k$ (for the block form)
results.conclusion: $A = U\Sigma V^\top$ with $U, V$ orthogonal and $\Sigma$ diagonal with $\sigma_1 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_{\min(m,n)} \ge 0$; at rank $k$, $A = U_1\Sigma_1V_1^\top + U_2\Sigma_2V_2^\top$

formalizations.usage: Apply `NLAlib.singularValues_last_eq_iInf` with its displayed hypotheses: **Variational form of the smallest singular value.** For `A : Matrix m n 𝕜`, `σ_{card n - 1}(A) = inf { ‖Ax‖₂ : ‖x‖₂ = 1 }` (the last singular value in the list indexed by the number of columns; for a wide matrix both sides are `0`, and for an empty `n` both sides are `0` by the real convention `inf ∅ = 0`).
For any `A : Matrix (Fin m) (Fin n) ℝ`, `obtain ⟨U, V, h⟩ := exists_isSVD A` gives `h : IsSVD A U V` (orthogonal `U`, `V` and `A = U * rectDiag (singularValues A) * Vᵀ`); no hypotheses.
formalizations.note: IsSVD A U V: Uᵀ U = 1, Vᵀ V = 1, A = U · rectDiag (singularValues A) · Vᵀ, where singularValues A : ℕ → ℝ is Mathlib's LinearMap.singularValues of toEuclideanLin A (zero-indexed, antitone, zero beyond the rank). Also uniqueness of σ, block split at k (IsSVD.eq_head_add_tail), AᵀA and AAᵀ diagonalisations, frobSq = Σσ², invariance under orthogonal factors and transpose.

formalizations.usage: From `h : IsSVD A U V` and a split index `k`; rewrites `A` as the head `U * rectDiag (σ masked to i < k) * Vᵀ` (the truncated SVD) plus the tail `U * rectDiag (σ masked to i ≥ k) * Vᵀ`.
Pass `hU : Uᵀ * U = 1`, `hV : Vᵀ * V = 1`, `τ` nonnegative (`hτ0`) and antitone (`hτ`), and `hA : A = U * rectDiag τ * Vᵀ`; gives `singularValues A k = τ k` for every `k < min m n`.
No hypotheses; gives `frobSq A = ∑ k ∈ Finset.range (min m n), singularValues A k ^ 2`.

results.title: Eckart–Young–Mirsky: best rank-k approximation
results.informal: Both minima are attained by the truncated SVD $\lbrack\!\lbrack A \rbrack\!\rbrack_k$: $$\min_{\operatorname{rank} B \le k} \|A - B\| = \sigma_{k+1}(A), \qquad \min_{\operatorname{rank} B \le k} \|A - B\|_F^2 = \sum_{i>k} \sigma_i^2.$$
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ with singular values $\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots \ge 0$
target rank $k$
results.conclusion: $\min_{\operatorname{rank} B \le k} \|A - B\| = \sigma_{k+1}(A)$ and $\min_{\operatorname{rank} B \le k} \|A - B\|_F^2 = \sum_{i>k} \sigma_i^2$, both attained by $\lbrack\!\lbrack A \rbrack\!\rbrack_k$

formalizations.usage: `specNorm (A - truncatedSVD A k) = singularValues A k` (attainment).
From `hB : B.rank ≤ k`; gives `singularValues A k ≤ specNorm (A - B)` (lower bound).
`IsLeast {v | ∃ B, B.rank ≤ k ∧ v = specNorm (A - B)} (singularValues A k)`.

results.notes: The extension proves the Frobenius minimum, attained by its actual truncated SVD, for every target rank and shape. The spectral-norm minimum remains a separate open component; this combined entry is not promoted by the Frobenius proof. Spectral form proved 2026-10-10 (lower bound via Weyl, attainment via the SVD); the Frobenius form is `eckart-young-frobenius`.

results.title: Weyl and Mirsky perturbation bounds for singular values
results.informal: For every $i$, $|\sigma_i(A+E) - \sigma_i(A)| \le \|E\|$, and $$\Big(\sum_i \big(\sigma_i(A+E) - \sigma_i(A)\big)^2\Big)^{1/2} \le \|E\|_F.$$
hypotheses: $A, E \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$
results.conclusion: $|\sigma_i(A+E) - \sigma_i(A)| \le \|E\|$ for every $i$, and $\Big(\sum_i \big(\sigma_i(A+E) - \sigma_i(A)\big)^2\Big)^{1/2} \le \|E\|_F$

formalizations.usage: Rectangular Mirsky: the entire absolute singular-value difference vector is weakly majorized by the perturbation singular list.

results.title: Courant–Fischer min-max and Rayleigh quotients
results.informal: For Hermitian $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $\lambda_k(A)=\max_{\dim_{\mathbb C}S=k}\min_{x\in S,\|x\|=1}\operatorname{Re}(x^*Ax)=\min_{\dim_{\mathbb C}S=n-k+1}\max_{x\in S,\|x\|=1}\operatorname{Re}(x^*Ax)$. In particular the extreme eigenvalues are the extrema of the Hermitian Rayleigh quotient; the real symmetric specialization uses $x^\top Ax$.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ Hermitian with $\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n$
$1\le k\le n$; dimensions are over $\mathbb C$ (or over $\mathbb R$ for the existing real specialization)
results.conclusion: $\lambda_k(A)=\max_{\dim S=k}\min_{\|x\|=1,x\in S}\operatorname{Re}(x^*Ax)=\min_{\dim S=n-k+1}\max_{\|x\|=1,x\in S}\operatorname{Re}(x^*Ax)$, with attained inner and outer extrema; $\lambda_{\max}$ and $\lambda_{\min}$ are the attained extrema of the Rayleigh quotient.

formalizations.usage: Apply `Matrix.IsHermitian.eigenvalues₀_le_of_forall_mem` with its displayed hypotheses: **Courant–Fischer, min-max half.** For Hermitian `A`, if `re (xᴴAx) ≤ c · re (xᴴx)` on a subspace `W` of codimension at most `k` (`card n ≤ dim W + k`), then the `k`-th largest eigenvalue satisfies `λ_k ≤ c`.

Apply `Matrix.IsHermitian.le_eigenvalues₀_of_forall_mem` with its displayed hypotheses: **Courant–Fischer, max-min half.** For Hermitian `A`, if `c · re (xᴴx) ≤ re (xᴴAx)` on a subspace `S` of dimension at least `k + 1`, then `c ≤ λ_k`.

Apply `Matrix.IsHermitian.exists_submodule_eigenvalues₀_mul_le` with its displayed hypotheses: **Courant–Fischer, attaining subspace for the max-min half**: there is a subspace of dimension at least `k + 1` (the span of the top `k + 1` eigenvectors) on which `λ_k · re (xᴴx) ≤ re (xᴴAx)`.

Apply `Matrix.IsHermitian.exists_submodule_le_eigenvalues₀_mul` with its displayed hypotheses: **Courant–Fischer, attaining subspace for the min-max half**: there is a subspace of codimension at most `k` (the span of the eigenvectors `k, k+1, …`) on which `re (xᴴAx) ≤ λ_k · re (xᴴx)`.

Apply `Matrix.IsHermitian.eigenvalues₀_eq_iSup_iInf` with its displayed hypotheses: **Courant–Fischer, max-min formula.** For Hermitian `A`, `λ_k = max_{dim S ≥ k+1} min_{0 ≠ x ∈ S} ρ(x)`, written with `⨆`/`⨅` (both attained) and the Rayleigh quotient `ρ = rayleighQuotient A`.

Apply `Matrix.IsHermitian.eigenvalues₀_eq_iInf_iSup` with its displayed hypotheses: **Courant–Fischer, min-max formula.** For Hermitian `A`, `λ_k = min_{codim W ≤ k} max_{0 ≠ x ∈ W} ρ(x)`, written with `⨅`/`⨆` (both attained) and the Rayleigh quotient `ρ = rayleighQuotient A`; codimension at most `k` is `card n ≤ dim W + k`.

results.title: Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse and its identities
results.informal: The general real Moore–Penrose inverse exists at every rank, is unique, and satisfies all four Penrose identities. It agrees with pinvL/pinvR when the respective Gram matrix is invertible. Its products are the orthogonal range projectors. Its norm is zero for the zero matrix and otherwise the reciprocal of the smallest positive singular value. For every A, $\|A^\dagger\|_F^2=\operatorname{tr}((AA^\top)^\dagger)$.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, over arbitrary finite index types
Full-column or full-row rank is required only for the ordinary inverse formulas
results.conclusion: $AA^\dagger A=A$, $A^\dagger AA^\dagger=A^\dagger$, $(AA^\dagger)^\top=AA^\dagger$, $(A^\dagger A)^\top=A^\dagger A$; the inverse is unique, and $\|A^\dagger\|=0$ when rank is zero, otherwise $1/\sigma_{\operatorname{rank}(A)}(A)$.

formalizations.usage: The unique Moore–Penrose inverse of a real rectangular matrix.

results.conclusion: The actual finite adaptive expectation satisfies $\mathbb E\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}R_k\le(1+\varepsilon)a$. For h>0 and a>0, $k\ge ra/(\varepsilon a+h)+r\log(\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}A/(\varepsilon a+h))$ gives error at most $(1+\varepsilon)a+h$. results.title: Lanczos three-term recurrence and tridiagonalization
results.informal: In exact arithmetic the Lanczos vectors are orthonormal, span $\mathcal{K}_q(A,b)$, and satisfy $$AQ_q = Q_qT_q + \beta_q\,q_{q+1}e_q^\top$$ with $T_q$ Jacobi (tridiagonal).

formalizations.usage: A **Lanczos decomposition**: an Arnoldi decomposition, used for symmetric `A` (then `T = Qᵀ A Q` is a Jacobi matrix, `LanczosDecomp.T`).

**The Lanczos three-term recurrence** (column form): for symmetric `A` and `j + 1 < q`, `A q_j = β_j q_{j−1} + α_j q_j + β_{j+1} q_{j+1}` (with `β_0 = 0`).

**The Lanczos relation** `A Q_q = Q_q T_q + β_q q_{q+1} e_qᵀ` (for `q ≥ 1`), with `β_q = t_{q,q−1}` and `q_{q+1}` the last column of a decomposition of size `q + 1`; together with `T_apply_eq_zero_of_one_lt_dist` (`T_q` symmetric tridiagonal for symmetric `A`) and `ArnoldiDecomp.hasOrthonormalCols`, `ArnoldiDecomp.range_Q` this is the Lanczos tridiagonalisation.

**Gauss (Lanczos) quadrature is exact for degree `< 2q`.** If `A` is symmetric, `Q` has orthonormal columns and `K_q(A,b) ⊆ range Q`, then for every polynomial `p` with `deg p < 2q`, `bᵀ p(A) b = (Qᵀb)ᵀ p(QᵀAQ) (Qᵀb)`.

**Error of Gauss (Lanczos) quadrature.** Let `A` be symmetric with spectrum in `[a, c]`, `Q` with orthonormal columns, `K_q(A,b) ⊆ range Q`, and `p` a polynomial of degree `< 2q` with `|f − p| ≤ E` on `[a, c]`.
**The Lanczos quadrature value is a Gauss rule**: `(Q_qᵀ b)ᵀ f(T_q) (Q_qᵀ b) = ‖b‖² ∑ᵢ f(θᵢ) (uᵢ)₁²` for every `f`.

**Gauss quadrature through the Jacobi matrix**: for symmetric `A`, `q ≥ 1` and `deg p < 2q`, `bᵀ p(A) b = ‖b‖² ∑ᵢ p(θᵢ) (uᵢ)₁²` with nodes `θᵢ` the eigenvalues of `T_q` and weights the squared first eigenvector components.

results.notes: Exactness up to degree 2q−1 holds for any orthonormal basis of a space containing K_q; the Lanczos recurrence is only needed to identify the nodes as Ritz values.

results.title: Stochastic Lanczos quadrature error bound
results.informal: Actual independent Rademacher probes combine the deterministic Lanczos compression error with the proved Hutchinson tail. General analytic rates retain the domain and magnitude parameters rho and M; relative rates require a PSD matrix function and positive trace.
hypotheses: $A=A^\top\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ has spectrum in [a,c], a<c; m>=1 probes have mutually independent Rademacher coordinates, and q>=1
For each probe z_i, $Q_i^\top Q_i=I$ and $\mathcal K_q(A,z_i)\subseteq\operatorname{range}Q_i$; $\widehat t=m^{-1}\sum_i(Q_i^\top z_i)^\top f(Q_i^\top A Q_i)(Q_i^\top z_i)$
Analytic case: $\rho>1$, F is complex-differentiable and $|F|\le M$ on the open Bernstein ellipse, and $F(t)=f(((c-a)t+c+a)/2)$ on [-1,1]. Lipschitz case: f is L-Lipschitz on [a,c]
Relative case: $B=f(A)\succeq0$, $\tau=\operatorname{tr}B>0$, $0<\varepsilon\le1$ and $\delta>0$
results.conclusion: With $D_q=4nM\rho^{1-2q}/(\rho-1)$ in the analytic case or $D_q=\pi Ln(c-a)/(4q)$ in the Lipschitz case, $\mathbb P\{|\widehat t-\operatorname{tr}B|>\eta+D_q\}\le2\exp[-m(256e^2)^{-1}\min(\eta^2/\|B\|_F^2,\eta/\|B\|)]$ for eta>=0. If $D_q\le\varepsilon\tau/2$ and $m\ge1024e^2\varepsilon^{-2}\log(2/\delta)$, relative failure is at most delta. Analytic q may be chosen with $q\ge(1+\log(8nM/(\varepsilon\tau(\rho-1)))/\log\rho)/2$ and q>=1; a positive scalar lower bound f_min gives the computable replacement $q\ge(1+\log(8M/(\varepsilon f_{\min}(\rho-1)))/\log\rho)/2$. Absolute and Lipschitz step budgets are separate proved variants. Early Krylov termination, q above the ambient dimension and zero-size cases are included; a condition-number-only step bound is asserted only for specified functions such as the inverse.

results.notes: The supplied compression-frame contract is fully covered by the analytic, Lipschitz and Rademacher proof family. Analytic rates use the explicit ellipse parameter and magnitude; positive-trace relative rates and a computable positive scalar lower-bound variant are included. The inverse has its separate Chebyshev endpoint-ratio rate. No construction or matrix-vector operation count is asserted for the supplied frames.

clauses.statement: For a real symmetric matrix with spectrum in the stated interval, orthonormal compression frames containing each probe's K_q give deterministic quadrature error at most twice the uniform degree-below-2q polynomial approximation error times the average squared probe norm.

For a nonempty finite family of independent Rademacher coordinates, analyticity and a magnitude bound M on the open Bernstein ellipse of parameter rho greater than one give the advertised additive threshold 4nM divided by rho to the power 2q minus one and rho minus one, with the Hanson-Wright tail coefficient one over 256e squared.

For the same actual Rademacher law, an L-Lipschitz function on the spectral interval gives the additive quadrature threshold pi L n times interval length divided by 4q and the same Hanson-Wright tail.

For a positive semidefinite matrix function with positive trace and relative epsilon in zero to one, paying half the relative budget with deterministic quadrature error and taking at least 1024e squared epsilon inverse squared log of 2 over delta probes gives relative failure probability at most delta.

A positive analytic approximation order q satisfying the advertised logarithmic bound involving n, M, rho and the positive trace supplies the relative deterministic budget; a positive lower bound on the scalar function supplies the stated computable replacement involving f_min.

The analytic logarithmic order bound also gives an absolute-error tail, while Lipschitz functions have separate absolute and relative order budgets and a relative order budget using a positive scalar lower bound.

The inverse function on a positive spectral interval has the separate Chebyshev quadrature rate in the square-root endpoint ratio; arbitrary analytic-function rates retain their explicit ellipse and magnitude parameters.

results.title: Sketch-and-solve least squares
results.informal: If $S$ is an $\varepsilon$-subspace embedding for $[A\ \ b]$ then $$\|A\tilde{x} - b\| \le \frac{1+\varepsilon}{1-\varepsilon}\min_x\|Ax - b\|.$$ With the AMM property the factor is $1+\varepsilon$ with $k = O(d/\varepsilon)$.

$S$ an $\varepsilon$-subspace embedding for $\operatorname{range}([A\ \ b])$
$\tilde{x} \in \operatorname{argmin}_x\|S(Ax - b)\|$
$0\le\varepsilon<1$.
results.conclusion: $\|A\tilde{x} - b\| \le \frac{1+\varepsilon}{1-\varepsilon}\min_x\|Ax - b\|$; with the AMM property the factor is $1+\varepsilon$ with $k = O(d/\varepsilon)$

results.title: Polynomial calculus of a symmetric matrix: ‖p(A)v‖ ≤ max|p(λᵢ)| ‖v‖
results.informal: For symmetric $A = U\Lambda U^\top$, $p(A) = U p(\Lambda) U^\top$, so $\|p(A)\| \le \max_i |p(\lambda_i)|$, $\|p(A)v\|^2 \le M^2\|v\|^2$ and $\|p(A)v\|_A^2 \le M^2\|v\|_A^2$ whenever $|p| \le M$ on the spectrum. The one lemma every Krylov rate reduces to.

$p \in \mathbb{R}[x]$ with $|p(\lambda_i)| \le M$ for all $i$

The absolute tail assumes t>=0, and the absolute-moment exponent is real p>0.

The grade vanishes exactly for the zero vector: `ν(A,b) = 0 ↔ b = 0`.

**Finite termination.** If `A` is invertible and `A x⋆ = c`, then for every `x₀` the error `x⋆ − x₀` lies in `K_ν(A, r₀)`, `r₀ = c − A x₀`, `ν = ν(A, r₀)`; so every Krylov method that minimises over `x₀ + K_q` is exact at `q = ν`.

clauses.statement: Over any field and arbitrary finite matrix labels, the vector-relative minimal polynomial is monic, has natural degree equal to the Krylov grade, and is the unique monic annihilator of that degree.

A polynomial annihilates the starting vector exactly when the vector-relative minimal polynomial divides it; the native polynomial-module annihilator ideal is generated by that polynomial, including zero vectors.
The Krylov space has dimension min(q,grade), and its first q powers are independent exactly when q is at most the grade, over an arbitrary scalar field.
The grade-sized Krylov space is invariant under the matrix and every later Krylov space equals it.
The vector-relative minimal polynomial divides the operator minimal polynomial, so the grade is at most its degree and the operator minimal-polynomial degree is at most the ambient dimension.
Grade zero is equivalent to a zero starting vector, and an invertible matrix's inverse image of the starting vector belongs to the grade-sized Krylov space, including empty dimension.

results.title: Arnoldi basis and Hessenberg matrices
results.informal: The Arnoldi basis $Q_q = [q_1,\dots,q_q]$ is the Gram–Schmidt orthonormalisation of $b, Ab, \dots, A^{q-1}b$; $H_q = Q_q^\top A Q_q \in \mathbb R^{q\times q}$ and $\underline H_q = Q_{q+1}^\top A Q_q \in \mathbb R^{(q+1)\times q}$. A matrix is upper Hessenberg if $h_{ij} = 0$ for $i > j+1$. Characterisations: $Q_q$ has orthonormal columns spanning $\mathcal K_q(A,b)$ when $q \le \nu$, $H_q$ and $\underline H_q$ are upper Hessenberg, $h_{j+1,j} = \|(I - Q_jQ_j^\top)Aq_j\| \ge 0$ with equality iff $j \ge \nu$, and the basis is unique up to signs (implicit-Q uniqueness: positive subdiagonal fixes it).
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$ (no symmetry), $b \in \mathbb R^n$, $q \in \mathbb N$
for orthonormality and the Hessenberg sign/uniqueness statements: $q+1 \le \nu(A,b)$ (no breakdown)
The uniqueness comparison basis $\tilde Q$ is a graded Krylov basis: its first $j$ columns span $\mathcal K_j(A,b)$ for each $j$
results.conclusion: $Q_q^\top Q_q = I$, $\operatorname{range}Q_q = \mathcal K_q(A,b)$, $H_q$ and $\underline H_q$ upper Hessenberg with $h_{j+1,j} > 0$ for $j < \nu$; any graded Krylov basis $\tilde Q$ with orthonormal columns, $\tilde Q e_1 = b/\|b\|$ and $\tilde Q^\top A\tilde Q$ upper Hessenberg with positive subdiagonal equals $Q_q$

mathlib_prereqs.note: Already used by `NLAlib.lanczosBasis`.
No Hessenberg predicate in Mathlib (grep for Hessenberg finds nothing).

results.notes: NLAlib's `lanczosMatrix A b q` is already the Arnoldi basis for every real A: `lanczos_apply_eq_zero_of_add_one_lt` proves QᵀAQ is upper Hessenberg without symmetry. So this entry is mostly naming (`arnoldiMatrix := lanczosMatrix`, `hessenberg A b q := Qᵀ A Q`, the extended (q+1)×q matrix) plus the positive-subdiagonal and uniqueness characterisations. Consumers: arnoldi-relation, fom-def, arnoldi-fa-error, lanczos-recurrence, gmres-def (the least-squares form ‖βe₁ − H̲_q y‖). Prove. Implement as the canonical witness `arnoldiDecomp A b q (h : q ≤ krylovGrade A b) : ArnoldiDecomp A b q` of the bundled decomposition in graded-krylov-basis-def; H is the structure's compression, not a separate definition.

formalizations.usage: An **Arnoldi decomposition** of `(A, b)` of size `q`: a matrix `Q` whose columns form a graded orthonormal Krylov basis.
The Hessenberg matrix `H_q = Q_qᵀ A Q_q` of an Arnoldi decomposition.
**`H_q` is upper Hessenberg**: `h_ij = 0` for `i > j + 1`, for every `A`.
**`H_q` is unreduced**: its subdiagonal entries `h_{j+1,j}` are nonzero.
**Positive normalisation fixes the decomposition**: two Arnoldi decompositions with `q_1 ⬝ b > 0` and positive subdiagonal `h_{j+1,j} > 0` are equal.
The matrix `Q_q` of the first `q` Arnoldi vectors.
The Arnoldi Hessenberg matrix `H_q = Q_qᵀ A Q_q`.
**The Arnoldi basis spans the Krylov space**: `range Q_q = K_q(A, b)`, with no hypothesis.
**The Arnoldi basis is orthonormal below the grade**: `Q_qᵀ Q_q = I` for `q ≤ krylovGrade A b`.
**The Arnoldi Hessenberg matrix is upper Hessenberg**, `h_ij = 0` for `i > j + 1`, for every `A` and every `q` (no symmetry, no non-breakdown hypothesis).
The **canonical Arnoldi decomposition** (Gram–Schmidt, positive subdiagonal) of size `q ≤ krylovGrade A b`.
**The canonical decomposition has positive subdiagonal**: `h_{j+1,j} = ‖g_{j+1}‖/‖g_j‖ > 0` with `g_j` the unnormalised Gram–Schmidt vectors.
**Characterisation of the canonical decomposition**: an Arnoldi decomposition with `q_1 ⬝ b > 0` and positive subdiagonal is the Gram–Schmidt one, `Q = arnoldiMatrix A b q`.

results.title: Arnoldi relation AQ_q = Q_qH_q + h_{q+1,q} q_{q+1} e_qᵀ
results.informal: With the Arnoldi basis, $$AQ_q = Q_{q+1}\underline H_q = Q_qH_q + h_{q+1,q}\,q_{q+1}e_q^\top,$$ and $Q_q^\top AQ_q = H_q$. Arnoldi breaks down at step $q$ ($h_{q+1,q} = 0$) iff $q = \nu(A,b)$, in which case $AQ_q = Q_qH_q$ and $\mathcal K_q$ is $A$-invariant. For symmetric $A$, $H_q = T_q$ is the symmetric tridiagonal Jacobi matrix and the relation is the Lanczos three-term recurrence $Aq_j = \beta_{j-1}q_{j-1} + \alpha_jq_j + \beta_jq_{j+1}$.
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $b \ne 0$, $1 \le q$
$q + 1 \le \nu(A,b)$ for the extended form (so $q_{q+1}$ exists); $q \le \nu$ and $h_{q+1,q} := 0$ otherwise
results.conclusion: $AQ_q = Q_qH_q + h_{q+1,q}q_{q+1}e_q^\top = Q_{q+1}\underline H_q$; $h_{q+1,q} = 0 \iff q = \nu(A,b)$; for $A = A^\top$: $H_q$ is symmetric tridiagonal and $Aq_j = \beta_{j-1}q_{j-1} + \alpha_jq_j + \beta_jq_{j+1}$ with $\beta_j = h_{j+1,j}$

mathlib_prereqs.note: Q Qᵀ x = x for x in the span; NLAlib already has the matrix form `mulVec_transpose_mulVec_of_mem_range`.

results.notes: Closes the open half of the existing candidate `lanczos-recurrence` (whose notes say the identity AQ_q = Q_qT_q + β_q q_{q+1}e_qᵀ is not yet stated); that entry should gain `depends_on: arnoldi-relation`. Column j of the identity is A q_j ∈ K_{j+1} = span(q_1..q_{j+1}) expanded in the orthonormal basis, so the proof is short given `range_lanczosMatrix` and the Hessenberg lemma. Consumers: lanczos-recurrence, fom-def, gmres-def (least-squares form), krylov-polynomial-exactness, arnoldi-fa-error, Lanczos-based SLQ (`slq-error`) when written with the recurrence. Prove. Round 8: A Q_q = Q_{q+1} H̲_q and A Q_q = Q_q H_q + h_{q+1,q} q_{q+1} e_qᵀ are proved for every ArnoldiDecomp of order q+1, with A Q = Q H ↔ grade = q.

formalizations.usage: **Column form of the Arnoldi relation**: `A q_j = ∑ᵢ h_ij qᵢ` whenever `j + 1 < q` (then `A q_j ∈ K_{j+2} ⊆ K_q`); by `H_apply_eq_zero_of_add_one_lt` only `i ≤ j + 1` contribute.
**`A Q_q = Q_{q+1} H̲_q`** with `H̲_q = Q_{q+1}ᵀ A Q_q` (the `(q+1) × q` Hessenberg matrix), with no hypothesis beyond the decomposition of size `q + 1`.
**The Arnoldi relation** (outer-product form): `A Q_q = Q_q H_q + q_{q+1} h̲ᵀ` where `h̲ = (h_{q+1,1}, …, h_{q+1,q})` is the last row of `H̲_q`.
**The Arnoldi relation** `A Q_q = Q_q H_q + h_{q+1,q} q_{q+1} e_qᵀ` (for `q ≥ 1`; `e_q` is the last unit vector of `ℝ^q`).
**Breakdown**: when `q` reaches the grade, `K_q` is `A`-invariant and the Arnoldi relation closes, `A Q_q = Q_q H_q`.
**Breakdown characterisation**: for `q ≥ 1`, the Arnoldi relation closes (`A Q_q = Q_q H_q`, `K_q` is `A`-invariant) iff `q` is the grade of `b`.
**The Lanczos three-term recurrence** (column form): for symmetric `A` and `j + 1 < q`, `A q_j = β_j q_{j−1} + α_j q_j + β_{j+1} q_{j+1}` (with `β_0 = 0`).

results.title: Krylov projection is exact on low-degree polynomials; the Ritz polynomial minimises ‖p(A)b‖
results.informal: If $Q$ has orthonormal columns with $\mathcal K_q(A,b) \subseteq \operatorname{range}Q$ and $H = Q^\top AQ$, then $p(A)b = Q\,p(H)\,Q^\top b$ for every $p$ with $\deg p < q$, and $Q^\top p(A)b = p(H)Q^\top b$ for $\deg p \le q$. If moreover $\operatorname{range}Q = \mathcal K_q(A,b)$ with $q \le \nu$, the characteristic polynomial $\chi_H$ is the unique monic $p$ of degree $q$ minimising $\|p(A)b\|$.
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$ arbitrary, $b \in \mathbb R^n$, $q \ge 1$
$Q \in \mathbb R^{n\times k}$ with $Q^\top Q = I$ and $\mathcal K_q(A,b) \subseteq \operatorname{range}Q$; $H = Q^\top AQ$
for the minimality clause: $\operatorname{range}Q = \mathcal K_q(A,b)$ and $q \le \nu(A,b)$
results.conclusion: $p(A)b = Q\,p(H)\,Q^\top b$ for $\deg p < q$; $Q^\top p(A)b = p(H)\,Q^\top b$ for $\deg p \le q$; $\|\chi_H(A)b\| = \min\{\|p(A)b\| : p \text{ monic}, \deg p = q\}$ with $\chi_H(A)b \perp \mathcal K_q$

mathlib_prereqs.note: Cayley–Hamilton for H gives χ_H(H) = 0, hence Qᵀχ_H(A)b = 0.
Minimiser over the affine set {A^q b + K_q} iff orthogonal to K_q.

results.notes: Both polynomial exactness identities are reused from FunctionApprox. The CharacteristicPolynomial module completes the advertised bundle: for an exact orthonormal Krylov range and q<=grade, card columns=q is derived, the compression characteristic polynomial is monic of degree q, its residual is orthogonal to Kq, it minimizes the squared residual norm among monic degree-q polynomials, and equality holds exactly for that polynomial. The matrix may be nonsymmetric; arbitrary finite index types and q=0 are included.

formalizations.usage: **Krylov projection is exact on polynomials of degree `< q`.** If `Q` has orthonormal columns and `K_q(A,b) ⊆ range Q`, then `Q p(QᵀAQ) Qᵀ b = p(A) b` for every `p` with `deg p < q`, for any square `A`.
**Lanczos-FA is exact on polynomials.** For symmetric `A`, `Q` with orthonormal columns and `K_q(A,b) ⊆ range Q`, `krylovFunApprox Q A p b = p(A) b` for every `p` with `deg p < q`.
**Compression commutes with polynomials of degree `≤ q`.** If `Q` has orthonormal columns and `K_q(A,b) ⊆ range Q`, then `Qᵀ p(A) b = p(QᵀAQ) Qᵀ b` for every `p` with `deg p ≤ q`, for any square `A`.
Cayley–Hamilton and compressed polynomial exactness make the characteristic residual's Q coordinates zero.
The compression characteristic residual is orthogonal to range Q, including the contained Krylov space.
Monic residuals split by Pythagoras into the compression characteristic residual and a smaller-degree residual.
The compression characteristic polynomial minimizes the squared residual norm among monic polynomials of degree card(columns Q).
If card(columns Q)≤grade, norm equality with the characteristic polynomial holds exactly when the competing monic polynomial equals it.

results.title: Block Krylov subspaces and their matrix-polynomial characterisation
results.informal: For $A \in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$ and $\Omega \in \mathbb R^{n\times s}$, $\mathcal K_q(A,\Omega) = \operatorname{range}[\Omega, A\Omega, \dots, A^{q-1}\Omega] = \sum_{j=1}^s \mathcal K_q(A,\omega_j) = \{\sum_{i<q}A^i\Omega C_i : C_i \in \mathbb R^{s\times s'}\}$. It contains $\operatorname{range}(p(A)\Omega)$ for every scalar polynomial $p$ with $\deg p < q$, is nested in $q$, satisfies $A\mathcal K_q \subseteq \mathcal K_{q+1}$, and has dimension at most $qs$. The rectangular form used for low-rank approximation is $\mathcal K_q(AA^\top, A\Omega) \ni \varphi(AA^\top)A\Omega$ for $\deg\varphi < q$.
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $\Omega \in \mathbb R^{n\times s}$, $q \in \mathbb N$ (rectangular case: $A \in \mathbb R^{m\times n}$ and the space $\mathcal K_q(AA^\top, A\Omega)$)
results.conclusion: $\mathcal K_q(A,\Omega) = \sum_j \mathcal K_q(A,\Omega e_j)$; $\operatorname{range}(p(A)\Omega) \subseteq \mathcal K_q(A,\Omega)$ for $\deg p < q$; $\mathcal K_q \subseteq \mathcal K_{q+1}$, $A\mathcal K_q \subseteq \mathcal K_{q+1}$, $\dim\mathcal K_q \le qs$
results.notes: Define as `⨆ j, krylovSpace A (fun r => Ω r j) q` so every single-vector lemma transfers. Consumers: polynomial-filter-range-finder, block-krylov-lra (Musco–Musco Thm 1), subspace-iteration-expected (q = 1 slice), randomized block Krylov trace estimation (Krylov-aware Hutch++). Prove.

formalizations.usage: The block Krylov subspace `K_q(A, Ω) = span {(A^i Ω) e_j : i < q, j ∈ s}`, the range of `[Ω, AΩ, …, A^(q−1)Ω]`.
The Krylov space of a single column is contained in the block space: `K_q(A, Ω e_j) ⊆ K_q(A, Ω)`.
The block Krylov space is the sum of the single-vector Krylov spaces of the columns: `K_q(A, Ω) = ∑_j K_q(A, Ω e_j)`.
Matrix-polynomial characterisation of the block Krylov space (valid for every `q`): `x ∈ K_q(A, Ω) ↔ x = ∑_j p_j(A) Ω e_j` for polynomials `p_j` of degree `< q`.
`range (p(A) Ω) ⊆ K_q(A, Ω)` for every scalar polynomial `p` with `deg p < q`: the form used by block Krylov low-rank approximation.
Block Krylov spaces are nested: `q ≤ q' → K_q(A, Ω) ⊆ K_{q'}(A, Ω)`.
`dim K_q(A, Ω) ≤ q s` for `Ω` with `s` columns.

results.title: Residual polynomials and the min–max quantity ε_k(S)
results.informal: $\mathcal P_k^0 = \{p \in \mathbb R[x] : \deg p \le k,\ p(0) = 1\}$ and, for $S \subseteq \mathbb C$, $\varepsilon_k(S) = \inf_{p\in\mathcal P_k^0}\sup_{z\in S}|p(z)|$. For any $A$, every $x \in x_0 + \mathcal K_k(A,r_0)$ has residual $b-Ax=p(A)r_0$ for some $p\in\mathcal P_k^0$, and every such polynomial residual has an affine-Krylov representative. If $A$ is invertible, membership of a specified $x$ is equivalent to this residual-polynomial condition, and $x-x_\star=p(A)(x_0-x_\star)$ when $Ax_\star=b$. $\varepsilon_k$ is antitone in $k$, monotone in $S$, attained for finite or compact $S$, and $\varepsilon_k([a,b]) = 1/T_k\big(\tfrac{b+a}{b-a}\big)$ for $0<a<b$.
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $b, x_0 \in \mathbb R^n$, $r_0 = b - Ax_0$, $k \in \mathbb N$
$S \subseteq \mathbb C$ (or $\subseteq \mathbb R$)
Invertibility of $A$ is required only for the converse at a specified $x$ and the error-polynomial identity.
results.conclusion: $x-x_0\in\mathcal K_k(A,r_0)\Rightarrow\exists p\in\mathcal P_k^0,\ b-Ax=p(A)r_0$; every $p\in\mathcal P_k^0$ has such an affine-Krylov representative; if $A$ is invertible, the implication is an equivalence for a specified $x$; $\varepsilon_{k+1}(S)\le\varepsilon_k(S)$; $S\subseteq S^\prime\Rightarrow\varepsilon_k(S)\le\varepsilon_k(S^\prime)$; the infimum is a minimum for finite $S$; $\varepsilon_k([a,b])=1/T_k(\frac{b+a}{b-a})$
results.notes: The residual-polynomial algebra and affine-Krylov realization are proved in Krylov/LinearSystems/ResidualPolynomial. The iff for a specified iterate correctly takes IsUnit A: for A=0 a residual cannot detect a nonzero nullspace displacement. The interval minimax value is supplied by isLeast_chebyshev_minimax. The set-dependent minimax monotonicity and attainment clauses remain open. Consumers include GMRES, MINRES, Chebyshev and Richardson iteration, and FOM.

formalizations.usage: **Residual-polynomial form of an affine Krylov iterate.** If `x − x₀ ∈ K_q(A, r₀)`, `r₀ = c − A x₀`, then `c − A x = p(A) r₀` for a residual polynomial `p` (`deg p ≤ q`, `p(0) = 1`).
**Every residual polynomial is realised in `x₀ + K_q`.** For `deg p ≤ q`, `p(0) = 1` there is `y ∈ K_q(A, r₀)` with `c − A (x₀ + y) = p(A) r₀`.
**Error form of the residual polynomial.** If `A x⋆ = c` and `x − x₀ ∈ K_q(A, r₀)`, then `x − x⋆ = p(A)(x₀ − x⋆)` for a residual polynomial `p`.
**Error form, converse.** If `A x⋆ = c`, every residual polynomial `p` is realised: some `y ∈ K_q(A, r₀)` has `x₀ + y − x⋆ = p(A)(x₀ − x⋆)`.
**Residual-polynomial characterisation of `x₀ + K_q`.** For invertible `A`, `x − x₀ ∈ K_q(A, r₀) ↔ ∃ p, deg p ≤ q ∧ p(0) = 1 ∧ c − A x = p(A) r₀`.

Apply `NLAlib.residualMinimaxError_mono` with its displayed hypotheses: Enlarging the domain increases residual minimax error, without boundedness assumptions.
Apply `NLAlib.residualMinimaxError_le_one` with its displayed hypotheses: The constant residual polynomial one gives the universal upper bound one.

Apply `NLAlib.exists_polynomialSupNorm_eq_residualMinimaxError` with its displayed hypotheses: A real residual polynomial attains the minimax error on every compact complex set, including finite and empty sets.

clauses.statement: Every affine-Krylov iterate has a degree-bounded residual polynomial with constant coefficient one, and every such polynomial has an affine-Krylov representative, for arbitrary real matrices.

For a specified iterate the residual-polynomial converse requires invertibility; the forward error-polynomial identity relative to a supplied exact solution needs no invertibility when the iterate lies in the affine Krylov space.
Residual minimax error is defined by an extended nonnegative uniform supremum over any complex set, decreases with the degree, increases with the domain, is at most one, and is zero on the empty set.

Every compact complex set, including finite and empty sets or sets with invisible coefficient directions, has an attaining real residual polynomial with the advertised degree and constant-coefficient constraints.
On a positive real interval embedded in the complex plane, the residual minimax value is exactly the reciprocal Chebyshev value, including degree zero.

results.title: GMRES iterate: residual minimisation over the Krylov space
results.informal:
$x_k$ is a GMRES iterate if $x_k \in x_0 + \mathcal K_k(A,r_0)$ and $\|b - Ax_k\|_2 \le \|b - Ax\|_2$ for all $x \in x_0 + \mathcal K_k(A,r_0)$. Characterisations: an iterate exists for every $A$; the residual $r_k$ is unique and $x_k$ is unique if $A$ is invertible; $r_k \perp A\mathcal K_k(A,r_0)$ (Petrov–Galerkin); $\|r_k\| = \min_{p\in\mathcal P_k^0}\|p(A)r_0\|$; $\|r_{k+1}\| \le \|r_k\|$; with Arnoldi, $\|r_k\| = \min_y\|\,\|r_0\|e_1 - \underline H_k y\|$; if $A$ is invertible, $r_
u = 0$ at the grade $
u = 
u(A,r_0)$. For symmetric $A$ this is MINRES.
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $b, x_0 \in \mathbb R^n$, $r_0 = b - Ax_0$, $k \in \mathbb N$ (complex form: $\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ with the Hermitian inner product)
results.conclusion: existence; uniqueness of $r_k$ (and of $x_k$ if $A$ invertible); $r_k \perp A\mathcal K_k$; $\|r_k\| = \min_{p\in\mathcal P_k^0}\|p(A)r_0\|$; $\|r_{k+1}\| \le \|r_k\|$; $\|r_k\| = \min_y\|\,\|r_0\|e_1 - \underline H_ky\|$; $A$ invertible $\Rightarrow r_{\nu(A,r_0)} = 0$

mathlib_prereqs.note: Existence of the minimiser (Hilbert projection) applied to the finite-dimensional subspace A·K_k.
Petrov–Galerkin characterisation r_k ⟂ A K_k.

results.notes: The real variational predicate, existence, residual orthogonality, uniqueness, polynomial characterization, monotonicity and termination at the grade are proved. The real reduced Arnoldi least-squares clause is proved under gmres-arnoldi-form. The complex form remains open, including the bridge identifying real data with the corresponding complex GMRES residual. This entry remains candidate because its full advertised real and complex contract is not yet covered.

formalizations.usage: `x` is a GMRES iterate: `x − x₀ ∈ K_q(A, r₀)` (`r₀ = c − A x₀`) and `x` minimises `‖c − A y‖²` over `x₀ + K_q(A, r₀)`.
**Petrov–Galerkin characterisation.** `x` is a GMRES iterate iff `x − x₀ ∈ K_q(A, r₀)` and the residual is orthogonal to `A K_q(A, r₀)`.
**Existence.** For every square `A`, right-hand side `c`, start `x₀` and `q` there is a GMRES iterate (a least-squares problem over `A K_q`; no hypothesis on `A`).
**The GMRES residual is unique**: two GMRES iterates for the same data have the same residual `c − A x`.
**The GMRES iterate is unique for invertible `A`.**.
**Polynomial form of the residual**: `c − A x = p(A) r₀` for a residual polynomial `p` (`deg p ≤ q`, `p(0) = 1`).
**GMRES beats every residual polynomial**: `‖r_q‖² ≤ ‖p(A) r₀‖²` for every `p` with `deg p ≤ q` and `p(0) = 1`.
**`‖r_q‖² = min_{p ∈ 𝒫_q⁰} ‖p(A) r₀‖²`**: the squared GMRES residual is the least value of `‖p(A) r₀‖²` over residual polynomials.
**GMRES residuals are nonincreasing**: for `q ≤ q'`, `‖r_{q'}‖² ≤ ‖r_q‖²`.
**Finite termination.** For invertible `A`, a GMRES iterate with `q` at least the grade `ν = krylovGrade A r₀` solves the system: `c − A x = 0`.

results.title: GMRES bound for diagonalisable A: ‖r_k‖ ≤ κ(V) ε_k(Λ) ‖r_0‖
results.informal: If $A = V\Lambda V^{-1}$ with $\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_i)$, then the GMRES residual satisfies $$\frac{\|r_k\|}{\|r_0\|} \le \min_{p\in\mathcal P_k^0}\|p(A)\| \le \kappa_2(V)\min_{p\in\mathcal P_k^0}\max_i|p(\lambda_i)|.$$ For normal $A$ ($V$ unitary) the factor is $1$, and the bound is then sharp in the worst case over $r_0$ (Greenbaum–Gurvits, Joubert).
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$ and $V \in \mathbb C^{n\times n}$ invertible, $\lambda \in \mathbb C^n$ with $A = V\operatorname{diag}(\lambda)V^{-1}$ over $\mathbb C$
$x_k$ a GMRES iterate (gmres-def)
results.conclusion: $\|r_k\| \le \|V\|_2\|V^{-1}\|_2\,\max_i|p(\lambda_i)|\,\|r_0\|$ for every real $p \in \mathcal P_k^0$; for $A$ normal, $\|r_k\| \le \max_i|p(\lambda_i)|\,\|r_0\|$

mathlib_prereqs.note: No matrix diagonalisability predicate; state with an explicit V and diagonal Λ.

results.notes: Audit 2026-10-24: native real GMRES is now bounded through an actual complex diagonalization, and through the actual complex spectrum in the real-normal case. The Greenbaum–Gurvits worst-case equality discussed in the informal motivation remains a separate later variant; it is not asserted by the displayed per-polynomial bound.

formalizations.usage: **GMRES bound for real diagonalisable `A`.** If `A = V diag(d) W` with `V W = 1` (so `W = V⁻¹` and the `dᵢ` are the eigenvalues), then for every residual polynomial `p` with `|p(dᵢ)| ≤ M`, `‖r_q‖ ≤ ‖V‖₂ ‖V⁻¹‖₂ M ‖r₀‖` (squared form).
Use this result: A real GMRES iterate satisfies the full complex-diagonalization residual bound for every real residual polynomial.
Use this result: A real normal matrix has the sharp condition-factor-one GMRES bound, using its actual complex spectrum.
Use this result: Polynomial evaluation through an actual diagonalization has the source eigenvector condition-factor bound, including empty matrices.
Use this result: A real polynomial on a normal complex matrix is bounded by its values on the actual complex spectrum.

clauses.statement: Every real residual polynomial gives the GMRES bound with an invertible complex eigenvector matrix and its spectral-norm condition factor.
For a real normal matrix the factor is one, with bounds on its actual complex spectrum.

results.title: Elman bound: GMRES for positive-real A
results.informal: If the symmetric part $M = (A + A^\top)/2$ is positive definite, then $$\|r_k\| \le \Big(1 - \frac{\lambda_{\min}(M)^2}{\|A\|_2^2}\Big)^{k/2}\|r_0\|.$$ The same bound holds for restarted GMRES($m$) after $k$ total steps, since each cycle contracts by the per-step factor.
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$ with $M = \tfrac12(A + A^\top) \succ 0$, $\alpha = \lambda_{\min}(M) > 0$, $\beta = \|A\|_2$
$x_k$ a GMRES iterate from $x_0$
results.conclusion: $\|r_k\| \le (1 - \alpha^2/\beta^2)^{k/2}\|r_0\|$; for GMRES($m$) restarted every $m$ steps, $\|r^{(j)}\| \le (1 - \alpha^2/\beta^2)^{jm/2}\|r_0\|$ after $j$ cycles
results.notes: Proof: ‖(I − ωA)r‖² ≤ (1 − 2ωα + ω²β²)‖r‖², take ω = α/β², and p(z) = (1 − ωz)^k ∈ P_k^0. Entirely real; no field of values needed (the complex form with dist(0, W(A)) in place of α is a variant under field-of-values-def). Consumers: restarted GMRES, gmres-bgt (it is the bound BGT sharpen), preconditioned nonsymmetric solves where the preconditioned operator is positive real. Prove.

results.title: MINRES bounds: spectral min–max and two indefinite intervals
results.informal: For symmetric invertible $A$, the minimal-residual (MINRES = GMRES) iterate satisfies $\|r_k\| \le \min_{p\in\mathcal P_k^0}\max_i|p(\lambda_i)|\,\|r_0\|$. If the spectrum lies in $[a,b]\cup[c,d]$ with $a<b<0<c<d$ and $b-a = d-c$, then $$\|r_{2k}\| \le 2\Big(\frac{\sqrt{|ad|}-\sqrt{|bc|}}{\sqrt{|ad|}+\sqrt{|bc|}}\Big)^k\|r_0\|,$$ in particular $2\big(\frac{\kappa-1}{\kappa+1}\big)^k$ for $[-d,-c]\cup[c,d]$, $\kappa = d/c$; for $A \succ 0$ with spectrum in $[a,b]$, $\|r_k\| \le 2\big(\frac{\sqrt b-\sqrt a}{\sqrt b+\sqrt a}\big)^k\|r_0\|$.
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$ symmetric and invertible, $x_k$ a GMRES iterate (gmres-def)
for the interval clauses: every eigenvalue in $[a,b]\cup[c,d]$, $a<b<0<c<d$, $d - c = b - a$ (resp. in $[a,b]$, $0<a<b$)
results.conclusion: $\|r_k\| \le \max_i|p(\lambda_i)|\,\|r_0\|$ for every $p \in \mathcal P_k^0$; $\|r_{2k}\| \le 2\big(\frac{\sqrt{|ad|}-\sqrt{|bc|}}{\sqrt{|ad|}+\sqrt{|bc|}}\big)^k\|r_0\|$; definite case $\|r_k\| \le 2\big(\frac{\sqrt b-\sqrt a}{\sqrt b+\sqrt a}\big)^k\|r_0\|$
results.notes: The symmetric spectral polynomial bound and definite Chebyshev rate are proved. The equal-width indefinite two-interval polynomial prerequisite two-interval-minimax is now proved, but its explicit MINRES consumer bound remains open. Consumers include preconditioned MINRES for saddle-point systems and regularized indefinite solves.

formalizations.usage: **MINRES spectral bound.** For symmetric `A` and every residual polynomial `p` (`deg p ≤ q`, `p(0) = 1`) with `|p(λᵢ)| ≤ M` at every eigenvalue, the GMRES (= MINRES) residual satisfies `‖r_q‖² ≤ M² ‖r₀‖²`.
**MINRES, definite case (Chebyshev rate).** If `A` is symmetric with every eigenvalue in `[a, b]`, `0 < a < b`, then `‖r_q‖ ≤ 2 ((√b − √a)/(√b + √a))^q ‖r₀‖` (squared form).

results.title: FOM (Arnoldi Galerkin) iterate and its residual formula
results.informal: $x_k^F$ is a FOM iterate if $x_k^F \in x_0 + \mathcal K_k(A,r_0)$ and $b - Ax_k^F \perp \mathcal K_k(A,r_0)$. It exists and is unique iff $H_k$ is invertible, and then $x_k^F = x_0 + \|r_0\|Q_kH_k^{-1}e_1$ and $r_k^F = -h_{k+1,k}\,(e_k^\top H_k^{-1}e_1)\|r_0\|\,q_{k+1}$. For symmetric positive definite $A$ the FOM iterate is the CG iterate.
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $b, x_0$, $r_0 = b - Ax_0 \ne 0$, $1 \le k \le \nu(A,r_0)$, Arnoldi data $Q_k, H_k, h_{k+1,k}, q_{k+1}$
results.conclusion: a FOM iterate exists uniquely iff $\det H_k \ne 0$; then $x_k^F = x_0 + \|r_0\|Q_kH_k^{-1}e_1$, $\|r_k^F\| = h_{k+1,k}\,|e_k^\top H_k^{-1}e_1|\,\|r_0\|$; if $A$ is symmetric positive definite, $x_k^F$ satisfies `IsCGIterate A b x₀ k`
results.notes: FOM is the Arnoldi approximation of f(A)b for f(z) = 1/z, so it ties the f(A)b entries to linear solves. Later variant (identity, difficulty 3): the Brown / Cullum–Greenbaum peak–plateau relation ‖r_k^F‖ = ‖r_k^G‖ / √(1 − (‖r_k^G‖/‖r_{k−1}^G‖)²), with FOM undefined exactly when GMRES stagnates (Saad 2003 §6.5.7). Consumers: lanczos-fa-error for 1/x, sketched FOM, the identification of CG as Galerkin (cg-convergence). Prove.

formalizations.usage: **FOM is the square system**: for `D : ArnoldiDecomp A r₀ q`, the residual of `x₀ + Q_q y` is orthogonal to `K_q(A, r₀)` (the Galerkin / FOM condition) iff `H_q y = Q_qᵀ r₀` (`= ±‖r₀‖ e₁`).
**For SPD `A` the FOM iterate is the CG iterate**: if `H_q y = Q_qᵀ r₀` then `x₀ + Q_q y` satisfies `IsCGIterate A c x₀ q`.

results.title: Chebyshev semi-iterative method: residual polynomial and rate
results.informal: For $A$ symmetric with spectrum in $[a,b]$, $0<a<b$, let $\theta = \tfrac{b+a}2$, $\delta = \tfrac{b-a}2$, $\sigma = \theta/\delta$, $\rho_0 = 1/\sigma$, $\rho_k = 1/(2\sigma - \rho_{k-1})$, $d_0 = r_0/\theta$, $d_k = \rho_k\rho_{k-1}d_{k-1} + \tfrac{2\rho_k}{\delta}r_k$, $x_{k+1} = x_k + d_k$. Then $r_k = R_k(A)r_0$ with $R_k(t) = T_k\big(\tfrac{\theta - t}{\delta}\big)/T_k(\sigma)$ (NLAlib `chebyshevResidual a b k`), so $$\|r_k\| \le \frac{\|r_0\|}{T_k(\sigma)} \le 2\Big(\frac{\sqrt b-\sqrt a}{\sqrt b+\sqrt a}\Big)^k\|r_0\|,$$ and the same for the error in the $A$-norm. No inner products are needed.
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$ symmetric with all eigenvalues in $[a,b]$, $0<a<b$
$x_0$ arbitrary and $x_k$ produced by the recurrence above (Saad Alg. 12.1)
results.conclusion: $b - Ax_k = R_k(A)(b - Ax_0)$ with $R_k = $ `chebyshevResidual a b k`; $\|r_k\| \le 2\big(\frac{\sqrt b-\sqrt a}{\sqrt b+\sqrt a}\big)^k\|r_0\|$ and $\|x_k - x_\star\|_A \le 2\big(\frac{\sqrt b-\sqrt a}{\sqrt b+\sqrt a}\big)^k\|x_0 - x_\star\|_A$

mathlib_prereqs.note: The three-term recurrence of T_k drives the identity r_k = R_k(A) r_0.

results.notes: The polynomially defined iterate, first step, residual and energy rates, and an equivalent three-term recurrence are proved. The coupled rho_k, d_k recursion stated above still needs an explicit realization bridge to that iterate; its exact reciprocal-Chebyshev residual bound also remains to be exposed. A polynomial specification alone does not complete the stated algorithm guarantee.

formalizations.usage: The Chebyshev iterate for spectrum in `[a, b]`: the polynomial method whose residual polynomial is `chebyshevResidual a b q = T_q((b + a − 2X)/(b − a)) / T_q((b + a)/(b − a))`, i.e. iteration polynomial `(1 − chebyshevResidual a b q) /ₘ X`.
**Chebyshev iteration, `A`-norm rate.** For symmetric `A` with spectrum in `[a, b]`, `0 < a < b`, and `A x⋆ = c`, `‖x_q − x⋆‖²_A ≤ (2((√b − √a)/(√b + √a))^q)² ‖x₀ − x⋆‖²_A`.
**Chebyshev iteration, residual rate.** For symmetric `A` with spectrum in `[a, b]`, `0 < a < b`, `‖c − A x_q‖² ≤ (2((√b − √a)/(√b + √a))^q)² ‖r₀‖²`.
**First Chebyshev step**: `x_1 = x₀ + r₀/θ`, `θ = (b + a)/2`, for `0 < a < b`.
**The Chebyshev three-term recurrence** (Saad Alg.

results.title: Preconditioned Richardson iteration: error contraction
results.informal: For $A, P$ symmetric positive definite with $aP \preceq A \preceq bP$ and step $\omega > 0$, the iteration $x_{k+1} = x_k + \omega P^{-1}(c - Ax_k)$ has $x_k - x_\star = (I - \omega P^{-1}A)^k(x_0 - x_\star)$ and $$\|x_k - x_\star\|_A \le \rho(\omega)^k\|x_0 - x_\star\|_A,\qquad \rho(\omega) = \max(|1-\omega a|, |1-\omega b|),$$ also in the $P$-norm; $\omega = 2/(a+b)$ gives $\rho = \frac{b-a}{b+a}$. $P = I$ is plain Richardson.
hypotheses: $A, P \in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$ symmetric positive definite, $0 < a \le b$, $aP \preceq A \preceq bP$ (Loewner)
$Ax_\star = c$, $\omega > 0$, $x_{k+1} = x_k + \omega P^{-1}(c - Ax_k)$
results.conclusion: $x_k - x_\star = (I - \omega P^{-1}A)^k(x_0 - x_\star)$; $\|x_k - x_\star\|_A \le \max(|1-\omega a|,|1-\omega b|)^k\|x_0 - x_\star\|_A$ (same in $\|\cdot\|_P$); with $\omega = \frac2{a+b}$ the factor is $\frac{b-a}{b+a}$

mathlib_prereqs.note: P^{1/2} to symmetrise P^{-1}A; or use LDL.lower_conj_diag for P = LLᵀ.

results.notes: The symmetrisation P^{-1/2}AP^{-1/2} with spectrum in [a,b] reduces it to polynomial-spectral-bound with p(t) = (1 − ωt)^k. Consumers: iterative sketching for least squares (Pilanci–Wainwright iterative Hessian sketch; Epperly 2024 'fast and forward stable' iterative sketching with P = (SA)ᵀ(SA), A ↦ AᵀA, a = (1+ε)^{-2}, b = (1−ε)^{-2} from `ose-def`), sketch-and-project viewed as preconditioned Richardson, damped Newton–sketch. Momentum (heavy-ball) acceleration is a later variant. Prove. Round 8: unpreconditioned form proved (weight g, optimal ω = 2/(a+b), rate (b−a)/(b+a)); preconditioned form open.

formalizations.usage: The Richardson iterate with step `ω`: `x_q = x₀ + ω ∑_{j<q} (I − ωA)^j r₀`, the polynomial method with residual polynomial `(1 − ωX)^q`; it satisfies `x_{q+1} = x_q + ω (c − A x_q)` (`richardsonIterate_succ`).

**Richardson contraction, weighted norm.** For symmetric `A` with spectrum in `[a, b]`, step `ω ≥ 0`, `A x⋆ = c` and a weight `g ≥ 0` on `[a, b]`, `‖x_q − x⋆‖²_{g(A)} ≤ ρ^{2q} ‖x₀ − x⋆‖²_{g(A)}` with `ρ = max(|1 − ωa|, |1 − ωb|)`.
**Richardson contraction, residual norm.** For symmetric `A` with spectrum in `[a, b]` and step `ω ≥ 0`, `‖c − A x_q‖² ≤ ρ^{2q} ‖r₀‖²`, `ρ = max(|1 − ωa|, |1 − ωb|)`.
**Richardson with the optimal step** `ω = 2/(a + b)`: for symmetric positive definite `A` with spectrum in `[a, b]`, `0 < a ≤ b`, `‖x_q − x⋆‖²_A ≤ ((b − a)/(b + a))^{2q} ‖x₀ − x⋆‖²_A`.

results.title: CGLS / LSQR convergence: κ(A)-rate for least squares
results.informal: For $A \in \mathbb R^{m\times n}$ of full column rank with singular values in $[\sigma_{lo},\sigma_{hi}]$, the iterate $x_k$ minimising $\|b - Ax\|$ over $x_0 + \mathcal K_k(A^\top A, A^\top(b - Ax_0))$ (CGLS/LSQR in exact arithmetic) satisfies $$\|A(x_k - x_\star)\| \le 2\Big(\frac{\sigma_{hi}-\sigma_{lo}}{\sigma_{hi}+\sigma_{lo}}\Big)^k\|A(x_0 - x_\star)\|,$$ $x_\star = \arg\min\|b - Ax\|$, and $\|b - Ax_k\|^2 = \|b - Ax_\star\|^2 + \|A(x_k - x_\star)\|^2$. With a right preconditioner $R$ the same holds with the singular values of $AR^{-1}$.
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb R^{m\times n}$ with $\operatorname{rank}A = n$, all singular values in $[\sigma_{lo},\sigma_{hi}]$, $0 < \sigma_{lo} \le \sigma_{hi}$
$x_k$ = `IsCGIterate (AᵀA) (Aᵀb) x₀ k`, equivalently the minimiser of $\|b - Ax\|$ over $x_0 + \mathcal K_k(A^\top A, A^\top(b - Ax_0))$
results.conclusion: $\|A(x_k - x_\star)\| \le 2\big(\frac{\sigma_{hi}-\sigma_{lo}}{\sigma_{hi}+\sigma_{lo}}\big)^k\|A(x_0 - x_\star)\|$ and $\|b - Ax_k\|^2 = \|b - Ax_\star\|^2 + \|A(x_k - x_\star)\|^2$

mathlib_prereqs.note: AᵀA ≻ 0 from full column rank.

results.notes: A direct instance of `quadForm_sub_le_of_isCGIterate(_of_le)` with A ↦ AᵀA, c = Aᵀb, a = σ_lo², b = σ_hi² (√ of the eigenvalue ratio is the singular value ratio). This is the Krylov solver of Blendenpik / LSRN / sketch-and-precondition: with R from a QR of SA and S an ε-embedding, κ(AR⁻¹) ≤ (1+ε)/(1−ε), so O(log(1/δ)) iterations suffice; the existing candidate `sketch-and-precondition` becomes an end-to-end result once this is in. Prove.

formalizations.usage: `x` is a `q`-th CGLS (equivalently, in exact arithmetic, LSQR) iterate for `min ‖b − A x‖` from `x₀`: it minimises `‖b − Ay‖²` over `x₀ + K_q(AᵀA, Aᵀ(b − Ax₀))`.
**CGLS is CG on the normal equations.** `x` is a CGLS iterate for `min ‖b − Ax‖` iff it is a CG iterate for `AᵀA x = Aᵀb` (same starting point, same Krylov space).
**Residual splitting for least squares.** If `x⋆` solves the normal equations `AᵀA x⋆ = Aᵀb`, then `‖b − Ax‖² = ‖b − Ax⋆‖² + ‖A(x − x⋆)‖²` for every `x`.

**CGLS/LSQR convergence, `κ(A)` rate.** Let `A : ℝ^{m×n}` have all singular values in `[σ_lo, σ_hi]`, `0 < σ_lo ≤ σ_hi`, stated as `σ_lo² ‖v‖² ≤ ‖Av‖² ≤ σ_hi² ‖v‖²` for all `v` (so `A` has full column rank), let `x⋆` solve the normal equations `AᵀA x⋆ = Aᵀb`, and `x` be a `q`-th CGLS iterate from `x₀`.
**CGLS/LSQR residual bound.** Under the hypotheses of `dotProduct_mulVec_sub_le_of_isCGLSIterate`, `‖b − Ax‖² ≤ ‖b − Ax⋆‖² + (2((σ_hi − σ_lo)/(σ_hi + σ_lo))^q)² ‖A(x₀ − x⋆)‖²`.

results.title: Preconditioned CG bound under a Loewner sandwich aP ≼ A ≼ bP
results.informal: For $A, P \succ 0$ with $aP \preceq A \preceq bP$, the PCG iterate (minimiser of $\|x - x_\star\|_A$ over $x_0 + \mathcal K_k(P^{-1}A, P^{-1}r_0)$) satisfies $$\|x_k - x_\star\|_A \le 2\Big(\frac{\sqrt b-\sqrt a}{\sqrt b+\sqrt a}\Big)^k\|x_0 - x_\star\|_A.$$ Equivalently CG applied to $L^{-1}AL^{-\top}$ for any factorisation $P = LL^\top$, with $\mathcal K_k(P^{-1}A, P^{-1}r_0) = L^{-\top}\mathcal K_k(L^{-1}AL^{-\top}, L^{-1}r_0)$.
hypotheses: $A, P \in \mathbb R^{n\times n}$ symmetric positive definite, $0 < a < b$ (or $\le$), $aP \preceq A \preceq bP$
$Ax_\star = c$; $x_k$ minimises `cgObjective A c` over $x_0 + \mathcal K_k(P^{-1}A, P^{-1}(c - Ax_0))$
results.conclusion: $\|x_k - x_\star\|_A \le 2\big(\frac{\sqrt b-\sqrt a}{\sqrt b+\sqrt a}\big)^k\|x_0 - x_\star\|_A$; the PCG Krylov space is the image under $L^{-\top}$ of the CG Krylov space of $L^{-1}AL^{-\top}$

mathlib_prereqs.note: LDLᵀ factorisation of a positive definite matrix gives P = LLᵀ after absorbing √D.
Alternative symmetric factor P^{1/2}.

results.notes: The Loewner-sandwich hypothesis is how randomized preconditioners are certified, so stating it that way avoids a generalised-eigenvalue API. Consumers: `nystrom-pcg` (Frangella–Tropp–Udell: (A + μI) vs Nyström preconditioner, a and b from the Nyström error), randomly pivoted Cholesky preconditioning, sketch-and-precondition when solved by CG on normal equations (with cgls-lsqr-bound). Prove.

formalizations.usage: **Krylov spaces under a change of variables:** `K_q(WB, Wv) = W K_q(BW, v)`.

`x` is a `q`-th preconditioned-CG iterate for `A x = c` with preconditioner `P`, started at `x₀`: it minimises `cgObjective A c` (equivalently the `A`-norm error) over `x₀ + K_q(P⁻¹A, P⁻¹(c − A x₀))`.
**PCG is CG on the split-preconditioned system.** If `Wᵀ P W = I` (so `P⁻¹ = WWᵀ`), then `x` is a PCG iterate for `(A, P, c, x₀)` iff `W⁻¹x` is a CG iterate for `WᵀAW ŷ = Wᵀc` from `W⁻¹x₀`.

**Preconditioned CG bound under a Loewner sandwich.** Let `P` be positive definite, `A` with `a P ≼ A ≼ b P` for `0 < a ≤ b` (so `A` is symmetric positive definite and `κ(P⁻¹A) ≤ b/a`), `A x⋆ = c`, and `x` a `q`-th PCG iterate from `x₀`.

results.title: Residual polynomial small on two intervals of equal length
results.informal: For $a<b<0<c<d$ with $d - c = b - a$ and $k \in \mathbb N$, $p(x) = R_k\big(x^2 - (b+c)x\big)$, with $R_k$ the shifted Chebyshev residual on $[\,|bc|, |ad|\,]$, has $\deg p \le 2k$, $p(0) = 1$ and $$\max_{x\in[a,b]\cup[c,d]}|p(x)| \le 2\Big(\frac{\sqrt{|ad|}-\sqrt{|bc|}}{\sqrt{|ad|}+\sqrt{|bc|}}\Big)^k.$$ The map $x \mapsto x^2 - (b+c)x$ sends both intervals onto $[\,|bc|, |ad|\,]$ and $0 \mapsto 0$. For $[-d,-c]\cup[c,d]$ the bound is $2\big(\frac{d-c}{d+c}\big)^k$.
hypotheses: $a < b < 0 < c < d$ with $d - c = b - a$, $k \in \mathbb N$
results.conclusion: $\exists p \in \mathbb R[x]$, $\deg p \le 2k$, $p(0) = 1$, $|p(x)| \le 2\big(\frac{\sqrt{|ad|}-\sqrt{|bc|}}{\sqrt{|ad|}+\sqrt{|bc|}}\big)^k$ for all $x \in [a,b]\cup[c,d]$
results.notes: Direct from `abs_eval_chebyshevResidual_le_two_mul_pow` with interval [|bc|, |ad|] composed with the quadratic (check: (d−b)(d−c) − bc = |ad| uses d − c = b − a). Optimality (it is the min–max value for equal-length intervals) is a later, harder variant. Belongs to the polynomial layer; group T2 may also list indefinite approximation, deduplicate on merge. Consumers: minres-bound, indefinite Lanczos-FA bounds, spectrum-slicing filters. Prove.

formalizations.usage: Apply `NLAlib.exists_degree_le_abs_eval_le_on_two_intervals` with positive inner endpoint and the requested degree to obtain the exact even/odd minimax relation under the quadratic folding map (see its indexed signature for this component's exact hypotheses).

results.title: Field of values (numerical range) and its basic properties
results.informal: $W(A) = \{x^*Ax : x \in \mathbb C^n, \|x\| = 1\}$ for $A \in \mathbb C^{n\times n}$ (for real $A$, of its complexification). Properties: compact; contains every eigenvalue; $W(A) \subseteq \{|z| \le \|A\|_2\}$; $W(\alpha A + \beta I) = \alpha W(A) + \beta$; $W(U^*AU) = W(A)$ for unitary $U$; $W(Q^*AQ) \subseteq W(A)$ for $Q$ with orthonormal columns (compressions, Arnoldi $H_q$); $\operatorname{Re}W(A) = [\lambda_{\min}(M), \lambda_{\max}(M)]$, $M = \tfrac12(A + A^*)$; convex (Toeplitz–Hausdorff); $W(A) = \operatorname{conv}\sigma(A)$ for normal $A$.
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb C^{n\times n}$ over a `Fintype` index (real $A$ via `A.map Complex.ofReal`)
Positive dimension for the displayed real-part closed interval; in dimension zero W(A) is empty and the other set clauses retain their empty meanings.
results.conclusion: $W(A)$ is compact and convex, $\sigma(A) \subseteq W(A) \subseteq \bar B(0,\|A\|_2)$, $W(Q^*AQ) \subseteq W(A)$ for $Q^*Q = I$, $\operatorname{Re}W(A) = [\lambda_{\min}(M),\lambda_{\max}(M)]$, and $W(A) = \operatorname{conv}\sigma(A)$ if $A$ is normal

mathlib_prereqs.note: Mathlib has no numerical range / field of values (grep for numericalRange, fieldOfValues, numericalRadius finds nothing).

results.notes: Intrinsically complex. Everything except convexity is difficulty 1–2; Toeplitz–Hausdorff convexity (reduce to 2×2) is the difficulty-3 piece and is not needed by the assumed consumers, so it can land last. Consumers: crouzeix-palencia, gmres-bgt, arnoldi-fa-error, the complex form of gmres-elman (dist(0, W(A)) in place of λ_min(M)), pseudospectral/numerical-range arguments in non-normal randomized NLA (e.g. sketched Arnoldi eigen-solvers). Prove.

formalizations.usage: Apply `NLAlib.numericalRange` with its displayed hypotheses: The numerical range of a complex matrix, defined using unit vectors in the Euclidean norm.
Apply `NLAlib.isCompact_numericalRange` with its displayed hypotheses: The numerical range is a compact image of the finite-dimensional unit sphere.
Apply `NLAlib.norm_le_specNorm_of_mem_numericalRange` with its displayed hypotheses: Every numerical-range point lies in the closed disk of radius the spectral norm.
Apply `NLAlib.spectrum_subset_numericalRange` with its displayed hypotheses: Every spectral point belongs to the numerical range: normalize a nonzero eigenvector.
Apply `NLAlib.numericalRange_smul_add_smul_one` with its displayed hypotheses: Affine transformations of matrices induce the same affine transformation of the numerical range.

clauses.statement: The numerical range is the quadratic-form image of the complex Euclidean unit sphere, compact in every finite dimension, includes the complex spectrum, and is contained in the spectral-norm closed disk; empty matrices have empty numerical range.
Affine scalar transformations give the affine image of the numerical range; unitary similarity preserves it; compression by any matrix with orthonormal columns only shrinks it.
In positive dimension the real projection of the numerical range is the interval between the extreme eigenvalues of the Hermitian part.
The numerical range of every finite complex matrix is convex (Toeplitz-Hausdorff), including empty dimension; a Bloch sphere proof establishes the two-dimensional compression case.
For every normal complex matrix the numerical range is exactly the convex hull of its complex spectrum, including repeated eigenvalues and empty dimension.

results.title: Crouzeix–Palencia: W(A) is a (1+√2)-spectral set
aliases: numerical range is a K-spectral set
results.informal: For every $A \in \mathbb C^{n\times n}$ and every polynomial $p$, $$\|p(A)\|_2 \le (1+\sqrt2)\max_{z\in W(A)}|p(z)|.$$ Consequently the GMRES residual satisfies $\|r_k\| \le (1+\sqrt2)\,\varepsilon_k(W(A))\,\|r_0\|$. (Crouzeix conjectures the constant 2.)
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $p \in \mathbb C[x]$
results.conclusion: $\|p(A)\|_2 \le (1+\sqrt2)\sup_{z\in W(A)}|p(z)|$; hence $\|r_k\| \le (1+\sqrt2)\min_{p\in\mathcal P_k^0}\max_{W(A)}|p|\,\|r_0\|$ for GMRES

results.notes: Assume (status `assumed` once a consumer is formalised): the statement is short, polynomial-only (no holomorphic functional calculus needed) and certain; the proof (Cauchy-transform / double-layer potential on the boundary of a convex set) is research-level to formalise. Stating it for polynomials sidesteps Mathlib's lack of a functional calculus for non-normal matrices. Consumers: arnoldi-fa-error, the GMRES field-of-values bound above, non-normal Krylov f(A)b and trace-of-f(A) estimators for nonsymmetric A.

results.title: Beckermann–Goreinov–Tyrtyshnikov sharpening of the Elman bound
results.informal: If $0 \notin W(A)$ and $\beta \in [0,\pi/2)$ is defined by $\cos\beta = \operatorname{dist}(0,W(A))/\|A\|_2$, then GMRES satisfies $$\|r_k\| \le \big(2 + \tfrac{2}{\sqrt3}\big)(2 + \gamma_\beta)\,\gamma_\beta^k\,\|r_0\|,\qquad \gamma_\beta = 2\sin\Big(\frac{\beta}{4 - 2\beta/\pi}\Big) < \sin\beta,$$ improving Elman's $\|r_k\| \le \sin^k\beta\,\|r_0\|$ in rate.
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb C^{n\times n}$ (or real, via complexification) with $0 \notin W(A)$
$\cos\beta = \operatorname{dist}(0,W(A))/\|A\|_2$, $\beta \in [0,\pi/2)$; $x_k$ a GMRES iterate

results.title: Greenbaum–Pták–Strakoš: any nonincreasing GMRES curve is possible
results.informal: Given $f(0) \ge f(1) \ge \dots \ge f(n-1) > 0$ and any nonzero $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n \in \mathbb C$, there are $A \in \mathbb C^{n\times n}$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ and $b$ such that GMRES from $x_0 = 0$ has $\|r_k\| = f(k)$ for $k = 0,\dots,n-1$. Eigenvalues alone say nothing about GMRES for non-normal $A$.
hypotheses: $n \ge 1$, $f : \{0,\dots,n-1\} \to (0,\infty)$ nonincreasing, $\lambda \in (\mathbb C\setminus\{0\})^n$
results.conclusion: $\exists A \in \mathbb C^{n\times n}, b \in \mathbb C^n$: $\operatorname{charpoly}A = \prod_i(x - \lambda_i)$ and the GMRES residuals with $x_0 = 0$ satisfy $\|r_k\| = f(k)$, $0 \le k \le n-1$

results.title: Best uniform approximation error E_n(f; [a,b])
results.informal: $E_n(f;[a,b]) = \inf\{E : \exists p,\ \deg p \le n,\ |f - p| \le E \text{ on } [a,b]\}$, written as an `sInf` in the `IsLeast` style of `isLeast_chebyshev_minimax`. For continuous $f$ the infimum is attained, decreases to $0$ (Weierstrass), and is invariant under affine change of variable.
hypotheses: $a < b$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$
$f$ continuous on $[a,b]$ (for attainment and convergence)
results.conclusion: there is $p^*$ with $\deg p^* \le n$ and $\max_{[a,b]}|f - p^*| = E_n(f)$; $E_{n+1}(f) \le E_n(f) \le \max_{[a,b]}|f|$ and $E_n(f) \to 0$; $E_n(f + p) = E_n(f)$ for $\deg p \le n$, $E_n(cf) = |c|\,E_n(f)$, $E_n(f+g) \le E_n(f) + E_n(g)$; $E_n(f;[a,b]) = E_n(f\circ\varphi;[-1,1])$ for the affine bijection $\varphi : [-1,1] \to [a,b]$

mathlib_prereqs.note: Weierstrass, ε-form: gives E_n(f) → 0

results.title: Lebesgue function and constant of polynomial interpolation
results.informal: For distinct nodes $x_0,\dots,x_n \in [a,b]$ with Lagrange basis $\ell_j$, $\lambda(x) = \sum_j |\ell_j(x)|$ and $\Lambda = \max_{[a,b]}\lambda$. $\Lambda$ is the operator norm of interpolation on $C[a,b]$, and interpolation is near-best: $\|f - p\| \le (1+\Lambda)E_n(f)$ (ATAP Thm 15.1).
hypotheses: $a < b$, nodes $v : \mathrm{Fin}(n+1) \to [a,b]$ injective, $\ell_j$ = `Lagrange.basis`
$f$ continuous on $[a,b]$ and $p$ its interpolant (`Lagrange.interpolate`) at $v$
results.conclusion: $\Lambda \ge 1$; $|p(x)| \le \lambda(x)\max_j |f(v_j)|$, with equality for some $f$ with $\max|f| = 1$, so $\Lambda$ is the operator norm of interpolation; $\max_{[a,b]}|f - p| \le (1 + \Lambda)\,E_n(f;[a,b])$

results.title: Convergence of Chebyshev series (ATAP Thm 3.1)
aliases: uniform convergence of the Chebyshev expansion
results.informal: If $f$ is Lipschitz on $[-1,1]$ then $\sum_k |a_k| < \infty$ and $f = \sum_k a_k T_k$ absolutely and uniformly. The working half: whenever $f$ is continuous and $\sum |a_k| < \infty$, $\max_{[-1,1]}|f - f_n| \le \sum_{k>n}|a_k|$.

results.title: Aliasing of Chebyshev polynomials and interpolant coefficients (ATAP Thms 4.1–4.2)
aliases: interpolation error at most twice the truncation tail
results.informal: On the Chebyshev grid $x_j=\cos(j\pi/n)$, $T_m,T_{2n\pm m},T_{4n\pm m},\ldots$ have identical sampled values. For an absolutely summable Chebyshev expansion, the interpolant coefficients are $c_0=a_0+a_{2n}+a_{4n}+\cdots$, $c_n=a_n+a_{3n}+a_{5n}+\cdots$, and $c_k=a_k+\sum_{\ell\ge1}(a_{2\ell n+k}+a_{2\ell n-k})$ for $1\le k<n$. Each alias fiber is counted once; $\max|f-p_n|\le2\sum_{k>n}|a_k|$.
hypotheses: $n \ge 1$, $0 \le m \le n$, grid $x_j = \cos(j\pi/n)$, $0 \le j \le n$ (Mathlib `Polynomial.Chebyshev.node n j`)
for the coefficient formula: $f$ continuous on $[-1,1]$ with $\sum_k |a_k| < \infty$, $p_n$ its interpolant in the grid with Chebyshev coefficients $c_k$
results.conclusion: $T_m(x_j) = T_{2\ell n + m}(x_j) = T_{2\ell n - m}(x_j)$ for all $\ell \ge 1$ and all $j$; $c_0 = a_0 + a_{2n} + a_{4n} + \cdots$, $c_n = a_n + a_{3n} + a_{5n} + \cdots$, and $c_k = a_k + \sum_{\ell \ge 1}(a_{2\ell n + k} + a_{2\ell n - k})$ for $1 \le k \le n-1$; consequently $\max_{[-1,1]}|f - p_n| \le 2\sum_{k > n}|a_k|$

mathlib_prereqs.note: cos(iπ/n): exactly ATAP's Chebyshev points
Chebyshev–Gauss quadrature at the zeros of T_n: the first-kind relative of the aliasing identity

results.notes: Thm 4.1 alone is difficulty 1 (T_k(cos(jπ/n)) = cos(kjπ/n)). ATAP states 4.2 for Lipschitz f; the summable hypothesis is what consumers have and avoids 3.1(b). First-kind variant at NLAlib's `chebyshevZero` (zeros of T_{n+1}): T_{2(n+1)-m} = -T_m there, and the same factor-2 bound holds. Consumers: the interpolant halves of chebyshev-approx-differentiable (4V) and chebyshev-approx-analytic (4M); Chebyshev-interpolation estimators of tr f(A). Prove. Coverage audit: Thm 4.1 (aliasing) is proved in NLAlib (`eval_T_node_eq_eval_T_alias`); Thm 4.2 only for analytic f.

results.title: Chebyshev equioscillation theorem (ATAP Thm 10.1)
results.informal: A continuous real $f$ on $[a,b]$ has a unique best approximation $p^* \in \mathcal{P}_n$, and $p$ with $\deg p \le n$ is $p^*$ iff $f - p$ equioscillates at $n+2$ points: $a \le x_0 < \cdots < x_{n+1} \le b$ with $f(x_i) - p(x_i) = \sigma(-1)^i\max_{[a,b]}|f - p|$.
hypotheses: $a < b$, $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $f$ continuous on $[a,b]$
$p \in \mathbb{R}[x]$ with $\deg p \le n$
results.conclusion: $\max_{[a,b]}|f - p| = E_n(f;[a,b])$ if and only if there are $a \le x_0 < \cdots < x_{n+1} \le b$ and $\sigma \in \{\pm 1\}$ with $f(x_i) - p(x_i) = \sigma(-1)^i\max_{[a,b]}|f - p|$ for all $i$; the best approximation is unique

results.title: De la Vallée Poussin lower bound for best approximation
results.informal: If $f - p$ ($\deg p \le n$) takes nonzero values of alternating sign at $n+2$ points of $[a,b]$, every polynomial of degree $\le n$ has error at least $\min_i |f(x_i) - p(x_i)|$ at one of those points, so $E_n(f) \ge \min_i|f(x_i) - p(x_i)|$.
hypotheses: $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $a \le x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_{n+1} \le b$
$p \in \mathbb{R}[x]$ with $\deg p \le n$ and $(f(x_i) - p(x_i))(f(x_{i+1}) - p(x_{i+1})) < 0$ for $0 \le i \le n$
results.conclusion: for every $q \in \mathbb{R}[x]$ with $\deg q \le n$, $\max_{0 \le i \le n+1}|f(x_i) - q(x_i)| \ge \min_{0 \le i \le n+1}|f(x_i) - p(x_i)|$; hence $E_n(f;[a,b]) \ge \min_i|f(x_i) - p(x_i)|$
results.notes: Proof: if q beat the minimum at every x_i, q - p would have the sign of f - p at the n+2 points, hence n+1 roots, hence q = p: contradiction. The discrete form needs no continuity of f. Consumers: equioscillation; explicit lower-bound certificates for approximating sign, exp and 1/x; generalises the lower half of chebyshev-minimax. Prove.

results.title: Polynomial approximation of sign(x) away from 0
results.informal: For $0 < \gamma < 1$ and $1 < r < \tfrac{1+\gamma}{1-\gamma}$ there is an odd $p(x) = x\,q(x^2)$ of degree $\le 2n+1$ with $|\operatorname{sgn} x - p(x)| \le \tfrac{2m_r^{-1/2}r^{-n}}{r-1}$ for $\gamma \le |x| \le 1$ (the $x^{-1/2}$ bound on $[\gamma^2, 1]$). results.title: Majorization and weak majorization of real vectors
results.informal: For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ write $s_k(x)=\sum_{i\le k}x_i^\downarrow$ for the sum of the $k$ largest entries. $x\prec_w y$ (weak majorization) iff $s_k(x)\le s_k(y)$ for $k=1,\dots,n$; $x\prec y$ iff moreover $s_n(x)=s_n(y)$. Characterisations: $x\prec y$ iff $x=Dy$ for a doubly stochastic $D$ iff $x\in\operatorname{conv}\{Py: P \text{ a permutation}\}$ (Hardy–Littlewood–Pólya); $x\prec y$ iff $\sum_i\varphi(x_i)\le\sum_i\varphi(y_i)$ for every convex $\varphi$; $x\prec_w y$ iff the same holds for every increasing convex $\varphi$.
hypotheses: $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ (index type `Fin n`, or any `Fintype` index)

results.title: Ky Fan maximum principle for eigenvalue and singular-value sums
aliases: sum of top-k eigenvalues as max trace
results.informal: For symmetric $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1\ge\dots\ge\lambda_n$ and $0\le k\le n$: $$\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i(A)=\max\{\operatorname{tr}(Q^\top AQ): Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times k},\ Q^\top Q=I_k\},$$ attained at any $k$ orthonormal top eigenvectors (dually, the bottom $k$ sum is the minimum). For $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$: $\sum_{i\le k}\sigma_i(A)=\max\{\operatorname{tr}(U^\top AV): U^\top U=V^\top V=I_k\}$. Corollary: $\sum_{i\le k}\lambda_i(A+B)\le\sum_{i\le k}\lambda_i(A)+\sum_{i\le k}\lambda_i(B)$, i.e. $\lambda(A+B)\prec\lambda(A)+\lambda(B)$, and $\sigma(A+B)\prec_w\sigma(A)+\sigma(B)$.
hypotheses: $A=A^\top\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, eigenvalues in decreasing order (`eigenvalues₀`)
$Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}$ with orthonormal columns
Singular-value form: $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $U\in\mathbb R^{m\times k}$, $V\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}$ with orthonormal columns, $k\le\min(m,n)$
results.conclusion: $\operatorname{tr}(Q^\top AQ)\le\sum_{i\le k}\lambda_i(A)$ with equality for top eigenvectors; $\operatorname{tr}(U^\top AV)\le\sum_{i\le k}\sigma_i(A)$ with equality for top singular vectors
