results.title: Unitarily invariant norms: von Neumann's gauge characterisation and Fan dominance
results.informal: A norm on $\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ is orthogonally (unitarily) invariant if $\|UAV\|=\|A\|$ for all orthogonal $U,V$. (von Neumann) These are exactly $\|A\|=\Phi(\sigma(A))$ for a symmetric gauge function $\Phi$ on $\mathbb R^{\min(m,n)}$, i.e. a norm invariant under permutations and sign changes. (Fan dominance) $\|A\|\le\|B\|$ for every orthogonally invariant norm iff $\|A\|_{(k)}\le\|B\|_{(k)}$ for every $k$, i.e. iff $\sigma(A)\prec_w\sigma(B)$.
hypotheses: $\|\cdot\|$ a norm on $\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ with $\|UAV\|=\|A\|$ for orthogonal $U\in O(m)$, $V\in O(n)$
For Fan dominance: $A,B\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$
results.conclusion: $\|A\|=\Phi(\sigma_1(A),\dots,\sigma_{\min(m,n)}(A))$ with $\Phi$ a symmetric gauge function, and conversely every symmetric gauge function defines such a norm; $\big(\forall\,\|\cdot\|\ \text{UI}:\ \|A\|\le\|B\|\big)\iff\forall k,\ \|A\|_{(k)}\le\|B\|_{(k)}$

Also absorbs the pinching inequality ‖∑ PᵢAPᵢ‖ ≤ ‖A‖ (Bhatia §IV.2, not proposed separately). results.title: Schur–Horn: the diagonal is majorized by the spectrum

Conversely (Horn) for every $d\prec\lambda$ there is a symmetric matrix with diagonal $d$ and spectrum $\lambda$ (a rotation of $\operatorname{diag}(\lambda)$).
hypotheses: $A=A^\top\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$

results.conclusion: $\operatorname{diag}(A)\prec\lambda(A)$; and every $d\prec\lambda$ is $\operatorname{diag}(Q\operatorname{diag}(\lambda)Q^\top)$ for some orthogonal $Q$

results.title: Lidskii–Wielandt: λ(A+B) − λ(A) ≺ λ(B), and Mirsky in every unitarily invariant norm
aliases: spectral variation in the nuclear norm
results.informal: For symmetric $A,B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ and every index set $J$ with $|J|=k$: $$\sum_{j\in J}\lambda_j(A+B)\le\sum_{j\in J}\lambda_j(A)+\sum_{i\le k}\lambda_i(B),$$ i.e. $\lambda(A+B)-\lambda(A)\prec\lambda(B)$. For singular values, $|\sigma(A+E)-\sigma(A)|\prec_w\sigma(E)$; hence $\|\operatorname{diag}(\sigma(A+E)-\sigma(A))\|\le\|E\|$ in every unitarily invariant norm, in particular $\sum_i|\lambda_i(A+E)-\lambda_i(A)|\le\|E\|_*$.
hypotheses: $A=A^\top$, $B=B^\top\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, eigenvalues decreasing
Singular-value form: $A,E\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$
results.conclusion: $\lambda(A+B)-\lambda(A)\prec\lambda(B)$ and $|\sigma(A+E)-\sigma(A)|\prec_w\sigma(E)$; $\sum_i|\lambda_i(A+E)-\lambda_i(A)|\le\|E\|_*$
results.notes: NLAlib's weyl-mirsky already has the spectral (Weyl) and Frobenius (Mirsky) cases for singular values; Lidskii is the general-index-set statement behind all unitarily invariant cases. The nuclear-norm corollary gives the 1-Wasserstein bound between empirical spectral distributions, W₁ ≤ ‖A − B‖_*/n, used in spectral-density estimation (slq-error / ctu21-type analyses). Recommendation: assume (statement is textbook-certain; Wielandt's minimax proof is long).

results.title: Horn's product inequality and weak majorization of σ(AB)
aliases: log-majorization of singular values of a product
results.informal: For $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times p}$, $B\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}$ and every $k$: $\prod_{i\le k}\sigma_i(AB)\le\prod_{i\le k}\sigma_i(A)\sigma_i(B)$ (Horn). Consequently (Weyl's majorant theorem) $\sum_{i\le k}\sigma_i(AB)^s\le\sum_{i\le k}\sigma_i(A)^s\sigma_i(B)^s$ for every $s>0$; in particular $\|AB\|_{(k)}\le\sum_{i\le k}\sigma_i(A)\sigma_i(B)$.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times p}$, $B\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}$ (`Fin` indices)
$1\le k\le\min(m,p,n)$, $s>0$

aliases: von Neumann trace inequality for symmetric matrices

results.title: Residual bounds for approximate eigenpairs (Krylov–Bogoliubov, Kato–Temple, one-vector sin θ)
aliases: quadratic accuracy of the Rayleigh quotient
results.informal: $A$ symmetric, $\|x\|=1$, $\rho=x^\top Ax$, $r=Ax-\rho x$. (a) For every $\mu\in\mathbb R$ some eigenvalue $\lambda$ satisfies $|\lambda-\mu|\le\|Ax-\mu x\|$; $\|r\|=\min_\mu\|Ax-\mu x\|$. (b) (Kato–Temple) if $\delta>0$ and $\lambda$ is the only eigenvalue in $(\rho-\delta,\rho+\delta)$ then $|\lambda-\rho|\le\|r\|^2/\delta$. (c) If $\delta=\min\{|\lambda'-\rho|:\lambda'\in\sigma(A)\setminus\{\lambda\}\}>0$ and $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projector onto the $\lambda$-eigenspace, $\|(I-P_\lambda)x\|\le\|r\|/\delta$. Also $\nabla_x\frac{x^\top Ax}{x^\top x}=\frac{2(Ax-\rho(x)x)}{x^\top x}$.
hypotheses: $A=A^\top\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $x\in\mathbb R^n$ with $x^\top x=1$
(b): $\delta>0$, $\sigma(A)\cap(\rho-\delta,\rho+\delta)=\{\lambda\}$
(c): $\delta=\operatorname{dist}(\rho,\sigma(A)\setminus\{\lambda\})>0$
results.conclusion: (a) $\min_{\lambda\in\sigma(A)}|\lambda-\mu|\le\|Ax-\mu x\|$; (b) $|\lambda-\rho|\le\|r\|^2/\delta$; (c) $\|(I-P_\lambda)x\|\le\|r\|/\delta$

results.title: Spectrum, singular values and norms of Kronecker products
results.informal: If $A=U_A\Sigma_AV_A^\top$ and $B=U_B\Sigma_BV_B^\top$ then $A\otimes B=(U_A\otimes U_B)(\Sigma_A\otimes\Sigma_B)(V_A\otimes V_B)^\top$, so its native domain-side singular-value multiset, including domain zeros, is the multiset of pairwise products of the two native domain-side lists (thin lists require the additional rectangular zero padding); hence $\|A\otimes B\|=\|A\|\|B\|$, $\|A\otimes B\|_F=\|A\|_F\|B\|_F$, $\operatorname{rank}(A\otimes B)=\operatorname{rank}A\cdot\operatorname{rank}B$, $(A\otimes B)^\dagger=A^\dagger\otimes B^\dagger$. For symmetric $A,B$ the eigenvalues of $A\otimes B$ are $\lambda_i(A)\lambda_j(B)$ and those of $A\otimes I+I\otimes B$ are $\lambda_i(A)+\lambda_j(B)$.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $B\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}$ (any `Fintype` indices; product index types)

results.title: Canonical (principal) angles between subspaces and sin Θ
results.informal: For $Q,\hat Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}$ with orthonormal columns, the canonical angles $0\le\theta_1\le\dots\le\theta_k\le\pi/2$ are defined by $\cos\theta_i=\sigma_i(Q^\top\hat Q)$ (so $\|\sin\Theta\|=\sin\theta_k=\sqrt{1-\sigma_k(Q^\top\hat Q)^2}$), and $\sin\Theta(Q,\hat Q)=\operatorname{diag}(\sin\theta_i)$. Characterisations, with $Q_\perp$ an orthonormal complement of $Q$: $\|\sin\Theta\|=\|Q_\perp^\top\hat Q\|=\|(I-QQ^\top)\hat Q\|=\|QQ^\top-\hat Q\hat Q^\top\|$; $\|\sin\Theta\|_F^2=k-\|Q^\top\hat Q\|_F^2=\tfrac12\|QQ^\top-\hat Q\hat Q^\top\|_F^2$; $\Theta$ depends only on the ranges, is symmetric in $(Q,\hat Q)$; if $\theta_k<\pi/2$, $\|\tan\Theta\|=\|(Q_\perp^\top\hat Q)(Q^\top\hat Q)^{-1}\|$.
hypotheses: $Q,\hat Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}$ with $Q^\top Q=\hat Q^\top\hat Q=I_k$
$Q_\perp\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-k)}$ with $[Q\ Q_\perp]$ orthogonal

results.title: Separation bound for the Sylvester operator X ↦ LX − XM
results.informal: Let $L\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$, $M\in\mathbb R^{q\times q}$ be symmetric and $X\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}$. (a) If $|\lambda_i(L)-\lambda_j(M)|\ge\delta>0$ for all $i,j$ then $\|LX-XM\|_F\ge\delta\|X\|_F$. (b) If the eigenvalues of $M$ lie in $[a,b]$ and those of $L$ lie outside $(a-\delta,b+\delta)$, $\delta>0$, then $\|LX-XM\|\ge\delta\|X\|$ (spectral norm; also Frobenius). The one-sided case $\lambda_{\max}(L)\le\alpha-\delta$, $\lambda_{\min}(M)\ge\alpha$ is the one used for top-$k$ subspaces.
hypotheses: $L=L^\top\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$, $M=M^\top\in\mathbb R^{q\times q}$, $X\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}$, $\delta>0$
(a) $\min_{i,j}|\lambda_i(L)-\lambda_j(M)|\ge\delta$
(b) $\sigma(M)\subseteq[a,b]$ and $\sigma(L)\cap(a-\delta,b+\delta)=\emptyset$
results.conclusion: (a) $\delta\|X\|_F\le\|LX-XM\|_F$; (b) $\delta\|X\|\le\|LX-XM\|$ and $\delta\|X\|_F\le\|LX-XM\|_F$
results.notes: Engine of both sin θ theorems; keeping it separate lets Davis–Kahan and Wedin share it. (a) is entrywise after diagonalising L and M (difficulty 2). (b) in the spectral norm needs the interval/one-sided structure (with arbitrary interlaced spectra the best constant is π/2, Bhatia–Davis–McIntosh; do not state that). The one-sided case follows from a shift and a positivity argument. Labels in bhatia97 §VII.2 to verify. Consumers: davis-kahan-sin-theta, wedin-sin-theta, eigenvalue-residual-bounds (k = 1 case). Recommendation: prove.

results.title: Davis–Kahan sin Θ theorem for invariant subspaces of symmetric matrices
results.informal: $A,\hat A=A+E\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ symmetric. $Q_1\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}$ orthonormal with $AQ_1=Q_1\Lambda_1$; $[\hat Q_1\ \hat Q_2]$ orthogonal with $\hat A\hat Q_i=\hat Q_i\hat\Lambda_i$. If $\sigma(\Lambda_1)\subseteq[a,b]$ and $\sigma(\hat\Lambda_2)\cap(a-\delta,b+\delta)=\emptyset$ with $\delta>0$, then $$\|\sin\Theta(Q_1,\hat Q_1)\|=\|\hat Q_2^\top Q_1\|\le\frac{\|\hat Q_2^\top EQ_1\|}{\delta}\le\frac{\|EQ_1\|}{\delta}\le\frac{\|E\|}{\delta},$$ and the same with Frobenius norms. Top-$k$ corollary: with $Q_1,\hat Q_1$ top-$k$ eigenvectors, $\|\sin\Theta\|\le\|E\|/(\lambda_k(A)-\lambda_{k+1}(\hat A))$ when the denominator is positive. Population-gap form (Yu–Wang–Samworth): if $g=\lambda_k(A)-\lambda_{k+1}(A)>0$ then $\|\sin\Theta\|_F\le2\min(\sqrt k\|E\|,\|E\|_F)/g$ and $\|\sin\Theta\|\le2\|E\|/g$.
hypotheses: $A=A^\top$, $E=E^\top\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $\hat A=A+E$
$Q_1\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}$ orthonormal, $AQ_1=Q_1\Lambda_1$; $[\hat Q_1\ \hat Q_2]$ orthogonal, $\hat A\hat Q_2=\hat Q_2\hat\Lambda_2$
$\delta>0$, $\sigma(\Lambda_1)\subseteq[a,b]$, $\sigma(\hat\Lambda_2)\cap(a-\delta,b+\delta)=\emptyset$
Population-gap form: $Q_1,\hat Q_1$ top-$k$ eigenvectors, $\lambda_k(A)>\lambda_{k+1}(A)$
results.conclusion: $\|\sin\Theta(Q_1,\hat Q_1)\|\le\|\hat Q_2^\top EQ_1\|/\delta\le\|E\|/\delta$ (also in $\|\cdot\|_F$); $\|\sin\Theta\|_F\le2\min(\sqrt k\|E\|,\|E\|_F)/(\lambda_k-\lambda_{k+1})$
results.notes: Proof: Q̂₂ᵀ(ÂQ₁ − Q₁Λ₁) = Λ̂₂(Q̂₂ᵀQ₁) − (Q̂₂ᵀQ₁)Λ₁ and ÂQ₁ − Q₁Λ₁ = EQ₁, then sylvester-separation-bound. The population-gap form: if ‖E‖ ≥ g/2 the bound is trivial (sin ≤ 1), otherwise Weyl (eigenvalue-perturbation-symmetric) gives λ_k(A) − λ_{k+1}(Â) ≥ g/2. Consumers: wedin-sin-theta; gap-dependent analyses of subspace-iteration-expected and block-krylov-lra; randomized PCA / spectral clustering from sketches; Nyström eigenvector accuracy (nystrom-randomized follow-ups); leverage scores of approximate eigenspaces (leverage-scores); random-start-power's gap form. Recommendation: prove. The population-gap corollaries use Yu–Wang–Samworth (2015), Theorem 2. results.title: Wedin's sin Θ theorem for singular subspaces
results.informal: $A,\hat A=A+E\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$; $U_1,V_1$ and $\hat U_1,\hat V_1$ the top-$k$ left/right singular vectors of $A$ and $\hat A$, $\hat\Sigma_1=\operatorname{diag}(\hat\sigma_1,\dots,\hat\sigma_k)$. With residuals $R=A\hat V_1-\hat U_1\hat\Sigma_1=-E\hat V_1$ and $S=A^\top\hat U_1-\hat V_1\hat\Sigma_1=-E^\top\hat U_1$, if $\delta:=\sigma_k(\hat A)-\sigma_{k+1}(A)>0$ then $$\max\{\|\sin\Theta(U_1,\hat U_1)\|,\|\sin\Theta(V_1,\hat V_1)\|\}\le\frac{\max\{\|R\|,\|S\|\}}{\delta}\le\frac{\|E\|}{\delta},$$ $$\sqrt{\|\sin\Theta(U_1,\hat U_1)\|_F^2+\|\sin\Theta(V_1,\hat V_1)\|_F^2}\le\frac{\sqrt{\|R\|_F^2+\|S\|_F^2}}{\delta}.$$ Population-gap form: if $g=\sigma_k(A)-\sigma_{k+1}(A)>0$ then both $\|\sin\Theta\|\le2\|E\|/g$.
hypotheses: $A,E\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ (`Fin` indices), $\hat A=A+E$, $1\le k\le\min(m,n)$
$U_1,V_1$ (resp. $\hat U_1,\hat V_1$) orthonormal top-$k$ singular vectors of $A$ (resp. $\hat A$)
$\delta=\sigma_k(\hat A)-\sigma_{k+1}(A)>0$

results.title: Wedin's perturbation bounds for the pseudoinverse and range projectors
results.informal: $A,B=A+E\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$. Identity: $$B^\dagger-A^\dagger=-B^\dagger EA^\dagger+B^\dagger B^{\dagger\top}E^\top(I-AA^\dagger)+(I-B^\dagger B)E^\top A^{\dagger\top}A^\dagger.$$ Bounds: if $\operatorname{rank}A=\operatorname{rank}B$ then $\|B^\dagger-A^\dagger\|\le\mu\|A^\dagger\|\|B^\dagger\|\|E\|$ with $\mu=\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$ (and $\|B^\dagger-A^\dagger\|_F\le\sqrt2\|A^\dagger\|\|B^\dagger\|\|E\|_F$); without the rank condition, $\|B^\dagger-A^\dagger\|\le\mu\max(\|A^\dagger\|^2,\|B^\dagger\|^2)\|E\|$. If $\operatorname{rank}A=\operatorname{rank}B$ and $\|A^\dagger\|\|E\|<1$: $\|B^\dagger\|\le\frac{\|A^\dagger\|}{1-\|A^\dagger\|\|E\|}$, and $\|AA^\dagger-BB^\dagger\|\le\min(\|A^\dagger\|,\|B^\dagger\|)\|E\|$.
hypotheses: $A,E\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $B=A+E$ (any `Fintype` indices; `moorePenroseInverse`)
Equal-rank forms: $\operatorname{rank}A=\operatorname{rank}B$
Inverse-norm form: $\|A^\dagger\|\|E\|<1$
results.conclusion: the three-term identity; $\|B^\dagger-A^\dagger\|\le\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\|A^\dagger\|\|B^\dagger\|\|E\|$ (equal rank); $\|AA^\dagger-BB^\dagger\|\le\min(\|A^\dagger\|,\|B^\dagger\|)\|E\|$ (equal rank)

results.title: Generalized Schur complement criterion for positive semidefinite block matrices
results.informal: For symmetric $M=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\B^\top&C\end{pmatrix}$ with $A\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$: $$M\succeq0\iff A\succeq0,\ (I-AA^\dagger)B=0,\ C-B^\top A^\dagger B\succeq0.$$ When $M\succeq0$, the Schur complement $M/A=C-B^\top A^\dagger B$ satisfies $x^\top(M/A)x=\min_{y}\begin{pmatrix}y\\x\end{pmatrix}^\top M\begin{pmatrix}y\\x\end{pmatrix}$ (attained at $y=-A^\dagger Bx$), and $0\preceq M/A\preceq C$.
hypotheses: $A=A^\top\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$, $B\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}$, $C=C^\top\in\mathbb R^{q\times q}$ (any `Fintype` indices, `Matrix.fromBlocks`)
$A^\dagger$ the Moore–Penrose inverse; no invertibility assumed

results.title: Löwner–Heinz and inverse antitonicity for real symmetric matrices
results.informal: For real symmetric $0\preceq A\preceq B$ and $r\in[0,1]$: $A^r\preceq B^r$ (in particular $A^{1/2}\preceq B^{1/2}$), and $A\mapsto A^r$ is operator concave on PSD matrices. If $0\prec A\preceq B$ then $B^{-1}\preceq A^{-1}$ and $\log A\preceq\log B$. ($A\preceq B\not\Rightarrow A^2\preceq B^2$; the range $r\in[0,1]$ is sharp.)

results.title: Spectral condition number: inverse-norm product when invertible, infinity when singular
results.informal: For a square real or complex matrix, $\kappa_2(A)=\|A\|_2\|A^{-1}\|_2$ when $A$ is invertible and $\kappa_2(A)=\infty$ otherwise. The value lies in $\mathbb R_{\ge0}\cup\{\infty\}$. On invertible matrices of positive dimension it equals the ratio of largest to smallest singular values; it is invariant under adjoint and inversion, and is at least one in positive dimension. For positive-definite real matrices it is the extreme eigenvalue ratio. For square invertible real matrices of positive dimension, the attained relative distance to singularity is $1/\kappa_2(A)$. The separate rectangular quantity `moorePenroseConditionNumber` is $\|A\|_2\|A^\dagger\|_2$, takes value zero at zero, and agrees with the real value of $\kappa_2$ on invertible square matrices.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb K^{n\times n}$ with $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ (`RCLike`), on a finite index type
The usual largest/smallest singular-value ratio requires invertibility and positive dimension; the lower bound $\kappa_2(A)\ge1$ requires nonempty indices
The eigenvalue-ratio and attained distance-to-singularity results are stated for real matrices of positive square dimension; the former assumes positive definiteness and the latter invertibility
The empty square matrix is invertible and has condition number zero; the separate Moore–Penrose quantity applies to rectangular matrices
results.conclusion: $\kappa_2(A)=\infty$ exactly when $A$ is singular; otherwise $\kappa_2(A)=\|A\|_2\|A^{-1}\|_2$, equal to $\sigma_1(A)/\sigma_n(A)$ in positive dimension. For invertible real $A$ of positive dimension, $\min\{\|E\|_2/\|A\|_2:A+E\text{ singular}\}=1/\kappa_2(A)$.
results.notes: The square spectral condition number is ENNReal-valued and records singularity as infinity. The total real-valued Moore–Penrose quantity remains available separately as moorePenroseConditionNumber; its rectangular invariances and positive-rank singular-value ratio do not assert finiteness of the square condition number on singular matrices. Distance to the singular set requires positive dimension, since that set is empty in dimension zero.

results.title: Normwise forward-error bounds for linear systems
results.informal: Let $A$ be invertible, $Ax=b\ne0$, and $(A+\Delta A)(x+\Delta x)=b+\Delta b$ with $\kappa(A)\frac{\|\Delta A\|}{\|A\|}<1$. Then $$\frac{\|\Delta x\|}{\|x\|}\le\frac{\kappa(A)}{1-\kappa(A)\frac{\|\Delta A\|}{\|A\|}}\Big(\frac{\|\Delta A\|}{\|A\|}+\frac{\|\Delta b\|}{\|b\|}\Big).$$ A posteriori: for any $\hat x$, $\frac{\|x-\hat x\|}{\|x\|}\le\kappa(A)\frac{\|b-A\hat x\|}{\|b\|}$.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ invertible, $b\ne0$, $Ax=b$
$\kappa(A)\|\Delta A\|/\|A\|<1$, $(A+\Delta A)(x+\Delta x)=b+\Delta b$
results.conclusion: $\|\Delta x\|/\|x\|\le\frac{\kappa}{1-\kappa\|\Delta A\|/\|A\|}(\|\Delta A\|/\|A\|+\|\Delta b\|/\|b\|)$ and $\|x-\hat x\|/\|x\|\le\kappa\|b-A\hat x\|/\|b\|$
results.notes: Consumers: cg-convergence and nystrom-pcg (turning residual stopping criteria into error guarantees), sketch-and-precondition, randomized-kaczmarz / sketch-and-project error-vs-residual statements, iterative refinement with sketched preconditioners. Recommendation: prove.

results.title: Wedin's perturbation bound for full-rank least squares
results.informal: $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ of full column rank, $x=\arg\min\|Ax-b\|$ with $x\ne0$, $r=b-Ax$. Let $\|\Delta A\|\le\varepsilon\|A\|$, $\|\Delta b\|\le\varepsilon\|b\|$, $\kappa(A)\varepsilon<1$, $y=\arg\min\|(A+\Delta A)y-(b+\Delta b)\|$, $s=(b+\Delta b)-(A+\Delta A)y$. Then $$\frac{\|x-y\|}{\|x\|}\le\frac{\kappa\varepsilon}{1-\kappa\varepsilon}\Big(2+(\kappa+1)\frac{\|r\|}{\|A\|\|x\|}\Big),\qquad\frac{\|r-s\|}{\|b\|}\le(1+2\kappa)\varepsilon.$$ First-order form: $\frac{\|x-y\|}{\|x\|}\le\varepsilon\big(\frac{2\kappa}{\cos\theta}+\kappa^2\tan\theta\big)+O(\varepsilon^2)$, $\sin\theta=\|r\|/\|b\|$.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $\operatorname{rank}A=n$, $b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $A^\top b\ne0$
$\|\Delta A\|\le\varepsilon\|A\|$, $\|\Delta b\|\le\varepsilon\|b\|$, $\kappa(A)\varepsilon<1$
results.conclusion: $\frac{\|x-y\|}{\|x\|}\le\frac{\kappa\varepsilon}{1-\kappa\varepsilon}\big(2+(\kappa+1)\frac{\|r\|}{\|A\|\|x\|}\big)$ and $\frac{\|r-s\|}{\|b\|}\le(1+2\kappa)\varepsilon$

results.title: Cholesky factorisation: existence and uniqueness
results.informal: Every real symmetric positive definite $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ has a unique factorisation $A=LL^\top$ with $L$ lower triangular and $L_{ii}>0$; $L_{11}=\sqrt{A_{11}}$ and the trailing block of $L$ is the Cholesky factor of the Schur complement $A_{22}-A_{21}A_{11}^{-1}A_{12}$; $\det A=\prod_iL_{ii}^2$. Every PSD $A$ has $A=LL^\top$ with $L$ lower triangular and $L_{ii}\ge0$ (not unique in general).
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ symmetric positive definite (index `Fin n`, or a linearly ordered `Fintype`)
Semidefinite form: $A\succeq0$
results.conclusion: $\exists!\,L$ lower triangular with positive diagonal and $A=LL^\top$; for $A\succeq0$, $\exists L$ lower triangular with nonnegative diagonal and $A=LL^\top$

formalizations.usage: **Cholesky factorization**: `A = L Lᵀ` with `L` lower triangular with positive diagonal.
A matrix with a Cholesky factorization is positive definite (`L` invertible, so `xᵀ A x = ‖Lᵀ x‖² > 0` for `x ≠ 0`).
**Uniqueness of the Cholesky factor**.

Positive-definite real matrices have a unique positive-diagonal triangular Cholesky factor, on every finite linearly ordered index type.
The determinant of a triangular Cholesky factorization is the product of the squared factor diagonals, including an empty product.

results.title: QR factorisation: existence and uniqueness
results.informal: Every $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ with $m\ge n$ factors as $A=QR$ with $Q\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $Q^\top Q=I_n$, and $R$ upper triangular with $R_{ii}\ge0$ (thin QR; a full QR has $Q$ orthogonal $m\times m$). If $\operatorname{rank}A=n$ then $R_{ii}>0$, the pair $(Q,R)$ is unique, $R^\top R=A^\top A$ (so $R^\top$ is the Cholesky factor of $A^\top A$), $QQ^\top$ is the orthogonal projector onto $\operatorname{range}A$, $\sigma_i(R)=\sigma_i(A)$ and $\kappa(R)=\kappa(A)$.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $m\ge n$ (`Fin` indices)
Uniqueness: $\operatorname{rank}A=n$ and $R_{ii}>0$
results.conclusion: $\exists Q,R$: $A=QR$, $Q^\top Q=I$, $R$ upper triangular with $R_{ii}\ge0$; unique with $R_{ii}>0$ under full column rank, and then $R^\top R=A^\top A$, $QQ^\top=AA^\dagger$, $\sigma(R)=\sigma(A)$
results.notes: Consumers: sketch-and-precondition (SA = QR, then κ(AR⁻¹)), haar-orthogonal (the Q factor of a Gaussian matrix with R_ii > 0 is Haar; needs uniqueness), rsvd-expected-error / hmt-9-1-spectral (Q = orth(Y); NLAlib currently uses polarFrame instead), leverage-scores (ℓᵢ = ‖Q_{i,:}‖²), block-krylov-lra. Recommendation: prove.

formalizations.usage: **Thin QR factorization**: `A = QR` with `Q : m × n` having orthonormal columns and `R : n × n` upper triangular.
A rectangular matrix is **upper trapezoidal** (upper triangular in the rectangular sense): `R i j = 0` whenever `j < i`.
Full QR over RCLike: A = Q * R, Q unitary and R upper trapezoidal; no shape or rank restriction.
**Thin QR from full QR**: if `n ≤ m`, the first `n` columns of `Q` and the first `n` rows of `R` form a thin QR.
The Gram matrix of every thin QR factor equals the original Gram matrix, even at deficient rank.
Qᴴ * A = R for thin QR over RCLike.
Aᴴ * A = Rᴴ * R for thin QR, including rank-deficient inputs; no positive-diagonal convention is imposed.
Aᴴ * A is invertible iff every diagonal entry of R is nonzero.
`range A = range Q` when `R` is invertible.
Under full column rank (nonzero diagonal of R), pinvL A = R⁻¹ * Qᴴ.
Under full column rank (nonzero diagonal of R), A⁺ = R⁻¹ * Qᴴ.
Under full column rank, Q * Qᴴ = A * A⁺ is the orthogonal range projector.
**Existence of a full QR** for every real `m × n` matrix, with no rank or shape hypothesis.
Two real thin QR factorizations with positive diagonal have equal Q and R factors.
Full QR over arbitrary finite indices with the triangular corner located by a specified column embedding.
For standard finite coordinates, full QR has its nonnegative upper-triangular factor in the first rows and zero rows below that corner.
A nonnegative upper-triangular QR diagonal is strictly positive under full column rank, also in empty dimension.
Full column rank gives a unique thin QR pair with positive upper diagonal.
Under full column rank, the QR frame projector is the actual Moore--Penrose orthogonal range projector.
Use the complete contract for qr factorisation: existence and uniqueness, or apply its documented component declarations for individual clauses.

results.title: Subspace iteration as a sequence of subspaces
results.informal: The $k$-th subspace iterate from a starting block $\Omega \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times s}$ is the subspace $\mathcal{S}_k = \operatorname{range}(A^k \Omega)$; any orthonormal $Q_k$ with $\operatorname{range} Q_k = \mathcal{S}_k$ is a basis the algorithm may carry, and the Ritz pairs are those of $Q_k^\top A Q_k$. Orthonormalisation does not change $\mathcal{S}_k$, and $\mathcal{S}_k \subseteq \mathcal{K}_{k+1}(A, \Omega)$ (block Krylov with the fixed polynomial $x^k$).
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$, $\Omega \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times s}$, $k \in \mathbb{N}$
results.conclusion: $\mathcal{S}_k = \operatorname{range}(A^k\Omega) \le \mathcal{K}_{k+1}(A,\Omega)$; the compression $Q_k^\top A Q_k$ is independent of the orthonormal basis $Q_k$ up to orthogonal similarity
results.notes: Design: the iterate is a subspace, every basis is a witness (docs/KRYLOV_DEFINITIONS.md §3.9). NLAlib already states the HMT power scheme on range((AAᵀ)^q A Ω) in LowRank/PowerIteration.lean; this entry names the object. Consumers: subspace-iteration-convergence, random-start-power, block-krylov-lra (comparison lemma S_k ≤ K_{k+1}).

formalizations.usage: The `k`-th subspace iterate `S_k = range (A^k Ω)` of subspace (orthogonal, simultaneous) iteration started from the block `Ω`.
One step of subspace iteration: `S_{k+1} = A S_k`.
Orthonormalisation does not change the iteration: if the columns of `Q` span `S_k` (for instance `Q` is an orthonormal basis of `S_k`), then `range (A Q) = S_{k+1}`.
Subspace iteration is block Krylov with the fixed polynomial `x^k`: `S_k = range (A^k Ω) ⊆ K_{k+1}(A, Ω)`.
Subspace iteration depends only on `range Ω`: `S_k(A, Ω R) = S_k(A, Ω)` for invertible `R`.

results.title: Matrix-vector query model of an algorithm
results.informal: An algorithm with matrix-vector access is an interaction tree: it is either an output, or a query vector $v$ with a continuation that receives $Av$ (adaptively). Its cost is the number of queries; its semantics on $A$ is obtained by answering every query with $Av$. A randomized algorithm is a tree-valued random variable. "$x_q$ is computable with $q$ matvecs" means some tree of cost $q$ outputs $x_q$ for every $A$; Gram–Schmidt and other work not touching $A$ is free.
results.conclusion: A syntax `MatvecAlg n α` with `run A : α` and `cost : ℕ`; realisation theorems `∃ alg, cost alg = q ∧ ∀ A, run A alg = iterate` for Arnoldi/Lanczos, GMRES, CG and subspace iteration
results.notes: Design (docs/KRYLOV_DEFINITIONS.md §3.10): runtime statements at the level randomized NLA uses them. Upper bounds are realisation theorems; this is also the only setting in which matvec lower bounds (Braverman–Hallman–Musco 2020, Simchowitz–El Alaoui–Recht 2018) can be stated. Arithmetic cost (flops) is deliberately out of scope: recorded as notes on entries, not formalised. Consumers: every Krylov predicate (cg-convergence, gmres-def, arnoldi-def) gets a realisation theorem; lower bounds are future candidates.

results.title: Graded (nested) Krylov basis: unique up to signs, tridiagonal compression
results.informal: $Q = [q_0,\dots,q_{q-1}]$ is a graded Krylov basis for $(A,b)$ if it has orthonormal columns and $\operatorname{span}(q_0,\dots,q_i) = \mathcal{K}_{i+1}(A,b)$ for every $i$. For $q \le \operatorname{grade}(A,b)$ it exists and is unique up to the sign of each column; $Q^\top A Q$ is unreduced upper Hessenberg, and a Jacobi matrix (symmetric tridiagonal with positive-or-negative nonzero off-diagonal) when $A$ is symmetric. $Q_{q}$ is the leading block of $Q_{q+1}$ and $T_q$ the leading principal submatrix of $T_{q+1}$.
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$, $b \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $q \le \operatorname{grade}(A,b)$
results.conclusion: existence; uniqueness up to $Q \mapsto Q D$ with $D$ diagonal $\pm1$; $Q^\top A Q$ unreduced Hessenberg, tridiagonal if $A = A^\top$; nesting of $Q_q, T_q$ in $Q_{q+1}, T_{q+1}$

mathlib_prereqs.note: one construction; the predicate is what theorems take

results.notes: Design: docs/KRYLOV_DEFINITIONS.md §3.11. The predicate, not the process, is what Jacobi-matrix theorems take; `arnoldiBasis` (positive subdiagonal) is one representative, and NLAlib's current `lanczosMatrix` with `lanczos_apply_eq_zero_of_add_one_lt` is the existing proof of the Hessenberg/tridiagonal part. Consumers: lanczos-recurrence, jacobi-matrix-identities, lanczos-orthogonal-polynomials, kaniel-paige-saad, finite-precision Lanczos statements. API (docs/KRYLOV_DEFINITIONS.md §3.12): bundle as `ArnoldiDecomp A b q` = {Q, graded} with `H := Qᵀ A Q` a definition, `LanczosDecomp` the symmetric abbreviation with `T := H`, `restrict` for nesting, `exists_sign` for uniqueness, and `arnoldiDecomp` (today's `lanczosMatrix`) as the canonical witness.

formalizations.usage: `Q` is a **graded orthonormal Krylov basis** of `(A, b)`: its columns are orthonormal and for every `i < q` the first `i + 1` columns span `K_{i+1}(A, b)`.
**Nesting**: `H_{q'}` is the leading principal `q' × q'` submatrix of `H_q`.
**Uniqueness up to signs**: two Arnoldi decompositions of the same size differ by a diagonal `±1` matrix, `Q' = Q diag(s)`.
**For symmetric `A`, `T_q` is tridiagonal**: `t_ij = 0` whenever `|i − j| > 1`.
**Existence of graded bases**: a graded orthonormal Krylov basis with `q` columns exists iff `q ≤ krylovGrade A b`.

results.title: Lanczos polynomials are the orthonormal polynomials of the spectral measure; T is its Jacobi matrix
results.informal: For symmetric $A$ and an arbitrary graded orthonormal basis $q_j=p_j(A)b$, the polynomials are orthonormal for the spectral measure, and the compressed matrix is their Jacobi matrix. Its coefficients $\alpha_j=q_j^\top A q_j$ and signed $\beta_{j+1}=q_{j+1}^\top A q_j$ give the three-term recurrence; $|\beta_{j+1}|$ is the norm of the next residual. The characteristic polynomial obeys $\chi_jp_0=(\prod_{i=1}^j\beta_i)p_j$.
hypotheses: $A$ symmetric, $\|b\|=1$, and a graded orthonormal basis of length $q\le\operatorname{grade}(A,b)$
For the recurrence $j+1<q$; for the characteristic-polynomial identity $j<q$. Arbitrary column signs are allowed, so $p_0=\pm1$
results.conclusion: $\int p_i p_j\,d\mu_b=\delta_{ij}$; $Xp_j=\beta_jp_{j-1}+\alpha_jp_j+\beta_{j+1}p_{j+1}$, with the previous term zero at $j=0$; $\det(xI-T_j)p_0=(\prod_{i=1}^j\beta_i)p_j(x)$. The positive canonical orientation with $q_0=b$ has $p_0=1$ and positive subdiagonal.
results.notes: The characteristic-polynomial identity includes p0 for arbitrary graded bases. Unit norm of b alone does not force p0=1. Signed recurrence coefficients specialize to residual norms for the canonical positive orientation; the formal API uses the signed version.

formalizations.usage: **The Lanczos polynomials are orthonormal for the spectral measure**: `∫ p_i p_j dμ_b = δ_ij` for `i < q` (and any `j`; `p_j = 0` for `j ≥ q`).

**Three-term recurrence of the Lanczos polynomials**: for symmetric `A` and `j + 1 < q`, `X p_j = β_j p_{j−1} + α_j p_j + β_{j+1} p_{j+1}`, so the Jacobi matrix `T` holds the recurrence coefficients of the orthonormal polynomials of `μ_b`.

**`det(x I − T_q)` is the monic orthogonal polynomial of degree `q`**: for symmetric `A`, `χ_q = charpoly T_q` (monic of degree `q`, `charpoly_T_monic`, `natDegree_charpoly_T`) is orthogonal in `μ_b` to every polynomial of degree `< q`.

**`det(x I − T_j)` is proportional to the Lanczos polynomial `p_j`**: `χ_j p_0 = β_1 ⋯ β_j p_j` with `χ_j = charpoly T_j` (`p_0 = ±1/‖b‖` is a constant; for `‖b‖ = 1` and the canonical signs this is `det(x I − T_j) = β_1 ⋯ β_j p_j(x)`).

results.title: Jacobi matrix identities: Gauss nodes and weights, Christoffel–Darboux, continued fraction, interlacing
results.informal:
Let $T_q=Q_q^	op A Q_q$ be the actual signed Lanczos compression, $M=\|b\|^2$ and $
u=\mu_b/M$. Its simple eigenvalues $	heta_i$ are the Gauss nodes, and $v_i(0)^2>0$ are the weights for $
u$; the original measure weights are $W_i=Mv_i(0)^2$. Thus $e_0^	op f(T_q)e_0=\sum_i v_i(0)^2f(	heta_i)$ and the original Gauss rule is $M$ times this value, with exactness through degree $2q-1$. For consecutive valid leading compressions, descending eigenvalues satisfy $	heta_i(T_{q+1})>	heta_i(T_q)>	heta_{i+1}(T_{q+1})$ for $0\le i<q$. The finite resolvent $r_q(z)=e_0^*(zI-T_q)^{-1}e_0$ is the Jacobi convergent of the normalized Stieltjes transform $\int(z-t)^{-1}\,d
u(t)$, and $Mr_q(z)=\sigma_q(z)/\chi_q(z)=\sum_i W_i/(z-	heta_i)$ off the actual node spectrum. The ordinary nested continued fraction is valid when every intermediate denominator is nonzero, in particular for nonreal $z$ or real $z$ above the spectrum. At real intermediate poles use the trailing/full determinant quotient, or the rational-function interpretation. For the actual polynomials $p_j$ orthonormal for $\mu_b$ and signed coupling $a_m$, $(x-y)\sum_{j<m}p_j(x)p_j(y)=a_m(p_m(x)p_{m-1}(y)-p_{m-1}(x)p_m(y))$. This multiplied identity holds for all $x,y$; division requires $x
e y$, and formal differentiation gives the positive confluent kernel. If the top monic norm is zero, use the monic Wronskian divided by $h_{m-1}$ instead of a nonexistent normalized $p_m$. At order zero the scalar approximant is zero and the empty characteristic denominator is one.
hypotheses: $A$ is real symmetric, $b\ne0$, $1\le q\le\operatorname{grade}(A,b)$, and $T_q$ is the actual compression of a graded Lanczos basis. The spectral measure $\mu_b$ has original mass $M=\|b\|^2$; squared first eigenvector coordinates integrate $\mu_b/M$.

Strict interlacing compares a size-$(q+1)$ decomposition with its leading size-$q$ restriction, so $q+1\le\operatorname{grade}(A,b)$ is required. The larger order may equal the grade; eigenvalues above are ordered nonincreasingly.

The normalized Christoffel–Darboux formula from a size-$q$ decomposition uses $1\le m<q$. A fully normalized top polynomial requires $h_m>0$; the monic norm-divided terminal formula requires only the preceding norms $h_0,\ldots,h_{m-1}>0$.

The ordinary complex resolvent and determinant quotient require $z\notin\operatorname{spec}(T_q)$. Literal nested division additionally requires every trailing-block determinant to be nonzero; this is derived for nonreal $z$ and for real $z$ above the spectrum. The divided kernel requires $x\ne y$; multiplied and confluent formulas cover the other cases.
Zero order is handled by the empty determinant and zero scalar fraction, with no first coordinate or normalized zero-mass measure.
results.conclusion: The actual Jacobi/Lanczos matrix gives simple Gauss nodes and positive normalized weights, original-mass quadrature exactness, strict consecutive interlacing, finite complex resolvent and continued-fraction identities, and multiplied/divided/confluent Christoffel–Darboux identities on their stated finite-order domains.
results.notes: The finite Jacobi convergent approximates the transform of the normalized measure; multiplying its resolvent by the original mass gives the original-measure second-kind ratio and Gauss partial fractions. This is not an assertion that a nonterminal finite convergent equals the full Stieltjes transform, or that an infinite continued fraction converges. A real intermediate nested-fraction pole is allowed by the robust determinant quotient when the final characteristic denominator is nonzero. Strict interlacing and arbitrary pole-free complex matrix partial fractions are proved; terminal normalization is excluded when the top norm vanishes.

formalizations.usage: Apply `NLAlib.LanczosDecomp.sum_sq_eval_poly_eq_confluent_and_pos` with its displayed hypotheses: The actual signed Lanczos polynomials have a strictly positive confluent Christoffel–Darboux kernel in every normalized positive-order range.
**Christoffel–Darboux identity** for the Lanczos polynomials: for symmetric `A` and `1 ≤ m < q`, `(x − y) ∑_{j<m} p_j(x) p_j(y) = β_m (p_m(x) p_{m−1}(y) − p_{m−1}(x) p_m(y))`.
**Cauchy interlacing, upper half**: the eigenvalues of `T_{q'}` (`q' ≤ q`, a leading principal submatrix of `T_q`) satisfy `θ_i(T_{q'}) ≤ θ_i(T_q)` (eigenvalues in non-increasing order).
**Cauchy interlacing, lower half**: `θ_{i + (q − q')}(T_q) ≤ θ_i(T_{q'})` for `q' ≤ q`; with `q' = q − 1` and the upper half, the eigenvalues of `T_{q−1}` interlace those of `T_q`.

**Golub–Welsch**: `e₁ᵀ f(T_q) e₁ = ∑ᵢ f(θᵢ) (uᵢ)₁²` with `(θᵢ, uᵢ)` the eigenpairs of `T_q`: the Gauss rule has the eigenvalues of `T_q` as nodes and the squared first components of its eigenvectors as weights.
**The Lanczos quadrature value is a Gauss rule**: `(Q_qᵀ b)ᵀ f(T_q) (Q_qᵀ b) = ‖b‖² ∑ᵢ f(θᵢ) (uᵢ)₁²` for every `f`.

clauses.statement: The actual canonical moment Jacobi compression has monic alpha diagonal and positive square-root monic-beta adjacent entries, and its normalized polynomials satisfy the corresponding three-term recurrence. Actual signed Lanczos T has its own diagonal and signed off-diagonal coefficient matrix.

Actual Lanczos eigenvalues and squared first eigenvector coordinates give the normalized Golub–Welsch rule, original starting-vector mass restores the original measure rule, and the first 2q moments are integrated exactly. Every node is simple and every first-coordinate weight is positive.
Consecutive actual leading signed Lanczos compressions strictly interlace whenever the larger valid decomposition exists, including its displayed grade terminal order.

The actual signed normalized Christoffel–Darboux identity holds after multiplying by x-y, and its formal derivative gives the strictly positive confluent identity. The generic monic norm-divided identity extends the kernel through zero-norm termination without a nonexistent normalized terminal polynomial.

The actual nonreal Jacobi resolvent is the literal nested complex fraction for arbitrary signed real coefficients, and every intermediate scalar Schur denominator is proved nonzero. The actual signed Lanczos matrix inherits this formula.

Cramer gives the robust trailing/full determinant quotient at every complex point, including real intermediate nested-fraction poles; the finite polynomial continuant is the actual characteristic denominator of every leading signed Lanczos compression.

The actual canonical finite Jacobi resolvent is the original-mass-normalized second-kind ratio and Gauss Stieltjes partial fraction, and its rooted moments match all original measure moments through degree 2n-1, including finite-support termination. No infinite analytic continued-fraction convergence is asserted.
At order zero the scalar approximant is zero and the empty characteristic denominator is one; no nonexistent first coordinate is used.

results.title: A Krylov minimiser beats every residual polynomial (class theorem)
aliases: polynomial bound for minimal-residual and minimal-error methods
results.informal: If $x$ minimises any $E$ over $x_0 + \mathcal{K}_q(A, r_0)$ then for every $p$ with $\deg p \le q$, $p(0)=1$: $E(x) \le E(x^\star + p(A)(x_0 - x^\star))$ (and the residual form $F(c - Ax) \le F(p(A) r_0)$). When the minimized objective is $E(y)=\|y-x^\star\|_{g(A)}^2$, for symmetric $A$ and a weight $g \ge 0$ on the spectrum, $\|x - x^\star\|_{g(A)}^2 \le \max_i |p(\lambda_i)|^2\, \|x_0 - x^\star\|_{g(A)}^2$: CG is $g = X$, MINRES is $g = X^2$, error-minimising methods $g = 1$.
hypotheses: $Ax^\star=c$ and $r_0=c-Ax_0$ (for the error comparison)
$x-x_0\in\mathcal K_q(A,r_0)$ and $E(x)\le E(x_0+y)$ for all $y\in\mathcal K_q$
$\deg p\le q$ and $p(0)=1$

formalizations.usage: **Finite termination of CG.** For positive definite `A` with `A x⋆ = c`, once `q` reaches the grade `ν(A, r₀)` of the initial residual, every `q`-th CG iterate is the solution `x⋆`.

results.title: Polynomial (fixed-polynomial) iterative method
results.informal: A polynomial method is $x = x_0 + s(A)\, r_0$ for an iteration polynomial $s$; its residual polynomial is $p = 1 - X s$, the error is $p(A)(x_0 - x^\star)$ and the residual $p(A) r_0$, and $x - x_0 \in \mathcal{K}_{\deg s + 1}$. Richardson and Chebyshev iteration are instances with explicit $s$.
hypotheses: $r_0=c-Ax_0$ and $p=1-Xs$; the error identity requires $Ax^\star=c$
For the weighted spectral bound: $A$ symmetric and the polynomial weight $g\ge0$ on the spectrum
results.conclusion: $x - x^\star = p(A)(x_0 - x^\star)$, $c - Ax = p(A) r_0$, $\|x - x^\star\|_{g(A)}^2 \le \max_{\sigma(A)} |p|^2\, \|x_0 - x^\star\|_{g(A)}^2$
results.notes: Design: KRYLOV_DEFINITIONS §3.6 (`polyIterate`). Consumers: richardson-iteration, chebyshev-iteration, polynomial-filter-range-finder.

formalizations.usage: The polynomial method with iteration polynomial `s`: `x₀ + s(A) r₀`, `r₀ = c − A x₀`.
The residual of a polynomial method is `(1 − X s)(A) r₀`.
The error of a polynomial method is `(1 − X s)(A)(x₀ − x⋆)` when `A x⋆ = c`.
For symmetric A, Ax⋆=c and a nonnegative polynomial weight on the spectrum, the polynomial iterate's weighted error is bounded by the residual polynomial's squared spectral envelope.

results.title: Lanczos-FA interpolates f at the Ritz values
aliases: Krylov approximation of f(A)b as interpolation
results.informal: For symmetric $A$ and $Q$ with orthonormal columns, at most $q$ of them, with $\mathcal{K}_q(A,b) \subseteq \operatorname{range} Q$: $Q f(Q^\top A Q) Q^\top b = p(A)\, b$ where $p$ is the polynomial interpolant of $f$ at the eigenvalues of $Q^\top A Q$ (the Ritz values). Consequently the approximant depends only on $\operatorname{range} Q$.
hypotheses: $A$ symmetric, $Q^\top Q = I$, $\mathcal{K}_q(A,b) \le \operatorname{range} Q$, $\#\text{cols}(Q) \le q$
results.conclusion: $Q f(T) Q^\top b = p(A) b$ with $p$ interpolating $f$ on $\sigma(T)$
results.notes: Design: KRYLOV_DEFINITIONS §3.9 face 2. Lagrange rather than Hermite interpolation (the Lagrange form holds whenever f and p agree on the spectrum of T; distinct Ritz values when q ≤ grade).

formalizations.usage: **Lanczos-FA interpolates at the Ritz values (general form).** If `p` has `deg p < q` and agrees with `f` at the eigenvalues of `T = QᵀAQ` (the Ritz values), then `krylovFunApprox Q A f b = p(A) b`.

**Lanczos-FA is the interpolant at the Ritz values.** If `Q` has at most `q` columns, then `krylovFunApprox Q A f b = p(A) b` for the Lagrange interpolant `p` of `f` at the distinct eigenvalues of `QᵀAQ`.

results.title: Every subspace has an orthonormal basis matrix
results.informal: For a subspace $S \le \mathbb{R}^m$ there is $Q \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times \dim S}$ with $Q^\top Q = I$ and $\operatorname{range} Q = S$; used to give every Krylov or block Krylov space an orthonormal basis with no hypothesis.
results.conclusion: $Q^\top Q = I$, $\operatorname{range} Q = S$
results.notes: Design: KRYLOV_DEFINITIONS §3.1 (`orthonormalBasisMatrix S`). Consumers: gmres-def (existence), block-krylov-subspace, subspace-iteration-def.

formalizations.usage: A canonical matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis of the subspace `S ⊆ ℝᵐ`, indexed by `Fin (finrank S)`; built from Mathlib's `stdOrthonormalBasis`.
`orthonormalBasisMatrix S` has orthonormal columns.
The columns of `orthonormalBasisMatrix S` span `S`: `range Q = S`.

results.title: Triangular matrices: closure, determinant, invertibility
results.informal: Upper/lower (unit) triangular predicates on $\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ over an ordered index; products and inverses of triangular matrices are triangular, $\det$ is the product of the diagonal, and a triangular matrix is invertible iff its diagonal is nonzero. Triangular systems are solved by substitution.
results.conclusion: closure under $\cdot$ and $^{-1}$; $\det = \prod_i t_{ii}$; invertible $\iff \forall i,\ t_{ii} \ne 0$

formalizations.usage: A **unit lower triangular** matrix: lower triangular with ones on the diagonal (the `L` of an LU factorization).
A **unit upper triangular** matrix: upper triangular with ones on the diagonal.
An upper triangular matrix is invertible iff its diagonal entries are all nonzero (the determinant is the product of the diagonal, `Matrix.det_of_isUpperTriangular`).
A lower triangular matrix is invertible iff its diagonal entries are all nonzero.
**Forward substitution** for `L x = b`, as a total recursion on the leading pivot: `x₀ = b₀ / L₀₀`, then solve the trailing system with right-hand side `b_{1:} − L_{1:,0} x₀`.
**Back substitution** for `U x = b`: forward substitution on the index-reversed system (the reversal `Fin.rev` turns an upper triangular matrix into a lower triangular one).
Realisation of forward substitution: for lower triangular `L` with nonzero diagonal, `L (forwardSubst L b) = b`.
Realisation of back substitution: for upper triangular `U` with nonzero diagonal, `U (backSubst U b) = b`.

mathlib_prereqs.note: abbreviation for BlockTriangular id; NLAlib uses it directly

results.notes: Mathlib has `Matrix.BlockTriangular`, `Matrix.det_of_upperTriangular`, `Matrix.BlockTriangular.inv`; the entry packages them for `Fin n` and names the substitution solve.

results.title: LU factorization: existence iff leading principal minors are nonzero, uniqueness
results.informal: $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ invertible has a factorization $A = LU$ with $L$ unit lower triangular and $U$ upper triangular iff every leading principal minor $\det A_{1..k,1..k}$ is nonzero; the factorization is then unique. One elimination step is the Schur complement: $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ b/a & I\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} a & c^\top \\ 0 & C - b c^\top/a\end{pmatrix}$.
hypotheses: $A$ invertible (for the iff); or just: all leading principal minors nonzero (for existence)
results.conclusion: $\exists!\,(L, U)$ with $A = LU$, $L$ unit lower, $U$ upper triangular

formalizations.usage: **LU factorization**: `A = L U` with `L` unit lower triangular and `U` upper triangular.
**Uniqueness of the LU factorization** of an invertible matrix.

Apply `NLAlib.exists_isLU_of_forall_leadingMinor_ne_zero` with its displayed hypotheses: **Existence of LU** when the leading principal minors of orders `1, …, n − 1` are nonzero (no condition on `det A` itself), on any linearly ordered finite index; on `Fin n` the witness is `lu A` (`isLU_lu_of_forall_leadingMinor_ne_zero`).

Apply `NLAlib.exists_isLU_iff_forall_leadingMinor_ne_zero` with its displayed hypotheses: **Existence of LU for invertible matrices**: an invertible `A` has an LU factorization iff all its leading principal minors are nonzero (and it is then unique, `IsLU.unique`).

results.notes: The predicate `IsLU A L U`; the Schur-complement step connects to generalized-schur-complement-psd.

results.title: Gaussian elimination realises LU: succeeds iff the pivots are nonzero
results.informal: Gaussian elimination without pivoting, as a total recursion on the leading pivot, succeeds iff every pivot (the $(1,1)$ entry of the successive Schur complements) is nonzero, equivalently iff every leading principal minor is nonzero; on success its output $(L, U)$ satisfies $A = LU$ (`IsLU`).
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$
results.conclusion: $\mathrm{LUSucceeds}\,A \iff \forall k,\ \det A_{1..k,1..k} \ne 0$; success $\Rightarrow$ `IsLU A (lu A).1 (lu A).2`

formalizations.usage: **Gaussian elimination without pivoting** (Doolittle LU) as a total recursion on the leading pivot: with `A = [[a, rᵀ], [c, C]]`, `L = [[1, 0], [c/a, L']]`, `U = [[a, rᵀ], [0, U']]` where `(L', U') = lu (C − c rᵀ/a)`.
**Success of Gaussian elimination**: every pivot (the `(1,1)` entry of `A` and of each successive Schur complement) is nonzero.
**Realisation of Gaussian elimination**: if every pivot is nonzero, `lu` returns an LU factorization.

Apply `NLAlib.luSucceeds_iff_forall_leadingMinor_ne_zero` with its displayed hypotheses: **Breakdown of Gaussian elimination**: elimination without pivoting succeeds iff every leading principal minor `det A(1:k,1:k)`, `k = 1, …, n`, is nonzero.

Apply `NLAlib.isLU_lu_of_forall_leadingMinor_ne_zero` with its displayed hypotheses: **Realisation of Gaussian elimination under the minimal hypothesis**: if the leading principal minors of orders `1, …, n − 1` are nonzero, `lu A` is an LU factorization (the last pivot is never divided by, so `det A` may vanish).

results.notes: Algorithm conventions: docs/ALGORITHM_CONVENTIONS.md (total recursion over Fin n, success predicate, realisation theorem).

results.title: LU with partial pivoting: PA = LU with |L| ≤ 1 for every invertible A
results.informal: For every invertible $A$ there is a permutation $P$ with $PA = LU$, $L$ unit lower triangular with $|l_{ij}| \le 1$, $U$ upper triangular; the elimination recursion that pivots on the largest entry of the current column never fails for invertible $A$ and produces such a factorization.
hypotheses: $A$ invertible
results.conclusion: $\exists P, L, U$: $PA = LU$, $|l_{ij}| \le 1$; the partial-pivoting recursion succeeds

formalizations.usage: **LU with row permutation**: `P A = L U` with `P = σ.permMatrix ℝ`, written as `A.submatrix σ id = L U` (row `i` of `PA` is row `σ i` of `A`; `Matrix.toMatrix_toPEquiv_mul` converts).
**Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting** as a total recursion.
**Success of partial pivoting**: every pivot (after the row swap) is nonzero.
**Realisation of partial pivoting**, for every square `A` (no invertibility hypothesis): `luPartialPivot A` is a factorization `PA = LU`.
**Bounded multipliers**: partial pivoting gives `|lᵢⱼ| ≤ 1`, for every `A`.
Partial pivoting succeeds iff `A` is invertible.
Every square matrix has a factorization `PA = LU` with `|lᵢⱼ| ≤ 1`.

results.notes: Existence for singular A holds too (with U possibly singular); state the invertible case first.

results.title: Growth factor of Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting is at most 2^{n−1}
results.informal: With partial pivoting, $\max_{ij} |u_{ij}| \le 2^{n-1} \max_{ij} |a_{ij}|$ (Wilkinson); the bound is attained.
hypotheses: $PA = LU$ produced by partial pivoting ($|l_{ij}| \le 1$)
results.conclusion: $\rho = \max|U| / \max|A| \le 2^{n-1}$

formalizations.usage: **Growth bound for partial pivoting, row form**: if `|aᵢⱼ| ≤ M` for all entries then row `i` of `U` satisfies `|uᵢⱼ| ≤ 2^i M` (each elimination step at most doubles the entries, since the multipliers are bounded by one).
**Growth factor of partial pivoting**: `max |uᵢⱼ| ≤ 2^{n−1} max |aᵢⱼ|`, stated with an entrywise bound `M` on `A`.
The actual partial-pivoting recursion attains Wilkinson's exponential growth, with its implemented tie rule.
In every positive dimension there is an input bounded entrywise by one whose computed upper factor contains an entry of magnitude `2^(N-1)`.

results.notes: Exact-arithmetic statement about the factors; no rounding model (finite precision is on hold). Formalized coverage: Combines the actual partial-pivot elimination bound with an explicit Wilkinson input attaining the bound for every positive dimension.

clauses.statement: Combines the actual partial-pivot elimination bound with an explicit Wilkinson input attaining the bound for every positive dimension.

results.title: Cholesky recursion succeeds iff A is symmetric positive definite, and realises A = LLᵀ
results.informal: The Cholesky recursion ($a \mapsto \sqrt a$, $b \mapsto b/\sqrt a$, continue on the Schur complement $C - bb^\top/a$) succeeds (every pivot $> 0$) iff $A$ is positive definite (for symmetric $A$); on success $L L^\top = A$ with $L$ lower triangular with positive diagonal, and $L$ is unique. For positive semidefinite $A$, pivoted (diagonal-pivoting) Cholesky never fails, stops after $\operatorname{rank} A$ steps and returns $L L^\top = A$.
hypotheses: $A$ symmetric
results.conclusion: $\mathrm{CholeskySucceeds}\,A \iff A \succ 0$; success $\Rightarrow$ `IsCholesky A (cholesky A)`; PSD: pivoted variant terminates at the rank

formalizations.usage: **The Cholesky recursion** on the leading pivot: for `A = [[a, cᵀ], [c, C]]`, `L = [[√a, 0], [c/√a, L']]` with `L' = cholesky (C − c cᵀ/a)` (`pivotSchur`; for a symmetric `A` the first row and column agree).
**Success of the Cholesky recursion**: every pivot (the `(1,1)` entry of `A` and of each successive Schur complement) is positive.
**Realisation of the Cholesky recursion**: for symmetric `A` with all pivots positive, `cholesky A` is the Cholesky factor.
**Breakdown of the Cholesky recursion**: for symmetric `A`, the recursion succeeds iff `A` is positive definite (Cholesky is the test for positive definiteness).

**Pivoted Cholesky factorization** `P A Pᵀ = L Lᵀ` with `P = σ.permMatrix`, written as `A.submatrix σ σ = L Lᵀ` (the pivots in order are `σ 0, σ 1, …`), `L` lower triangular with nonnegative diagonal.

**Cholesky with diagonal pivoting** as a total recursion: swap the largest diagonal entry to the front (`diagPivotSwap`), take one Cholesky step, recurse on the Schur complement and permute the computed column by the later pivots.
**Pivoted Cholesky never fails on a positive semidefinite matrix**: `choleskyPivoted A` is a pivoted Cholesky factorization.

Apply `NLAlib.exists_choleskyPivoted_positive_prefix` with a positive semidefinite matrix and column index to identify the positive pivot prefix and zero columns after its rank (see its indexed signature for this component's exact hypotheses).
Use this explicitly catalogued scaffold only where its deferred hypothesis is accepted.
Use this explicitly catalogued scaffold only where its deferred hypothesis is accepted.

mathlib_prereqs.note: PSD form; the PD pivot criterion is proved in NLAlib by completing the square (`posDef_iff_pivotSchur`)

results.notes: Uses `Matrix.PosDef.fromBlocks₁₁` (Schur complement positivity) for the iff. Consumers: partial-cholesky-nystrom, preconditioned-cg (P^{1/2}), sylvester-inertia. The concrete pivoted Cholesky recursion is used. Positive pivots form a prefix, zero Schur tails produce zero trailing columns, and rank is counted only after this support invariant is established.

results.title: k steps of pivoted Cholesky equal the Nyström approximation on the pivot set
results.informal: For $A \succeq 0$ and pivots $S = \{s_1,\dots,s_k\}$ chosen in order, the partial Cholesky factor $F_k \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times k}$ satisfies $F_k F_k^\top = A(:,S)\,A(S,S)^{\dagger}\,A(S,:)$ (the column Nyström approximation) and the residual $A - F_k F_k^\top$ is the Schur complement of $A(S,S)$, again positive semidefinite with zero rows/columns on $S$.
hypotheses: $A \succeq 0$, any pivot sequence (zero or repeated pivots allowed; $0^{-1} = 0$)
results.conclusion: $F_k F_k^\top = A(:,S) A(S,S)^\dagger A(S,:)$; residual $= A / A(S,S) \succeq 0$

formalizations.usage: The **residual of partial Cholesky** after the pivots `s 0, …, s (k−1)`, in this order.
The **partial Cholesky factor** `F ∈ ℝ^{n×k}`: column `j` is `R(:, s j) / √R(s j, s j)` with `R` the residual after the first `j` pivots.
The partial Cholesky residual of a PSD matrix is PSD (each step is a Schur complement).
The partial Cholesky residual of a PSD matrix vanishes on the pivot rows.
The partial Cholesky residual of a PSD matrix vanishes on the pivot columns.
**Partial Cholesky residual identity**: `A − F Fᵀ` is the residual, for PSD `A` and any pivot sequence.
Use this explicitly catalogued scaffold only where its deferred hypothesis is accepted.
**The partial Cholesky residual is the generalized Schur complement**: `R = A − A(:,S) A(S,S)⁺ A(S,:)`, for PSD `A` and any pivot sequence.

results.notes: The deterministic heart of RPCholesky; the random pivot rule is layered on top in LowRank. D-A (round 9): holds for every pivot sequence of a PSD matrix; the positivity hypothesis was dropped. The PSD premise on A remains required. Zero or repeated pivots are permitted; this drops positive-pivot premises, not positive semidefiniteness of A.

results.title: Gram–Schmidt (classical and modified) realises the thin QR; breakdown iff a dependent column
results.informal: Classical and modified Gram–Schmidt on the columns of $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, as recursions, produce $Q$ with orthonormal columns and upper triangular $R$ with $A = QR$ and $r_{jj} > 0$; step $k$ breaks down iff $a_k \in \operatorname{span}(a_1,\dots,a_{k-1})$ (in exact arithmetic CGS and MGS give the same $Q, R$). $Q$ is the graded orthonormal basis of the column flag.
hypotheses: $A$ with linearly independent columns (for no breakdown)
results.conclusion: $A = QR$, $Q^\top Q = I$, $R$ upper triangular with positive diagonal; breakdown at $k \iff \operatorname{rank} A_{:,1..k} < k$

formalizations.usage: The working columns of **modified Gram–Schmidt** after `k` steps (Trefethen–Bau Alg.
The `Q` factor of modified Gram–Schmidt (the working columns after `n` steps).
The `R` factor of modified Gram–Schmidt: `r_ij = q_iᵀ w_j^{(i)}` for `i < j` (the working column `j` before step `i`), `r_ii = ‖w_i^{(i)}‖`.
**MGS = CGS in exact arithmetic**: modified Gram–Schmidt computes the same `Q` and `R` as classical Gram–Schmidt, for every `A` (breakdowns included).
**Realisation of modified Gram–Schmidt**: when Gram–Schmidt succeeds (linearly independent columns), MGS produces a thin QR of `A`.
The `j`-th **Gram–Schmidt vector** `q_j = v_j / ‖v_j‖` with `v_j = a_j − ∑_{i<j} (q_iᵀ a_j) q_i` (well-founded recursion on `j`).
The **Gram–Schmidt residual** `v_j = a_j − ∑_{i<j} (q_iᵀ a_j) q_i`.
The `Q` factor of classical Gram–Schmidt: column `j` is `q_j`.
The `R` factor of classical Gram–Schmidt: `r_ij = q_iᵀ a_j` for `i < j`, `r_jj = ‖v_j‖`, zero below the diagonal.
**Gram–Schmidt succeeds**: no residual `v_j` vanishes (every pivot `r_jj = ‖v_j‖` is positive).
**`QR = A` for classical Gram–Schmidt**, for every `A` (no success hypothesis: after a breakdown `q_j = 0` and `r_jj = 0`, and `a_j` is still `∑_{i<j} r_ij q_i`).
**The Gram–Schmidt columns are orthonormal or zero**, for every `A`: `QᵀQ = diag(1 if v_j ≠ 0, 0 if v_j = 0)`.
`Q` has orthonormal columns when Gram–Schmidt succeeds.
**Realisation of classical Gram–Schmidt**: when it succeeds, `(gramSchmidtQ A, gramSchmidtR A)` is a thin QR of `A` (with `r_jj > 0`, `gramSchmidtR_apply_self_pos`).
**Breakdown at step `j` iff `a_j` depends on the earlier columns**: `v_j = 0` iff `a_j ∈ span(a_i : i < j)`, for every `A` (no assumption on the earlier steps).
**Gram–Schmidt succeeds iff the columns of `A` are linearly independent.** Trefethen–Bau 1997, Thm 7.2 (full rank case); Golub–Van Loan 2013, §5.2.7.
`Q` is a **graded orthonormal basis of the column flag of `A`**: `Q` has orthonormal columns and, for each `k`, its first `k + 1` columns span the first `k + 1` columns of `A`.
**Gram–Schmidt spans the column flag**: `span(q_0, …, q_k) = span(a_0, …, a_k)` for every `k` and every `A` (zero columns after a breakdown do not change the span).
The column-flag property in the `IsGradedKrylovBasis` (`castLE`) form.
**The Gram–Schmidt `Q` is the graded basis of the column flag** when the process succeeds.
**Every thin QR with invertible `R` is a graded basis of the column flag**: `A = QR` with `R` upper triangular and `R_ii ≠ 0` gives `span(q_0, …, q_k) = span(a_0, …, a_k)`.
Use this explicitly catalogued scaffold only where its deferred hypothesis is accepted.

results.notes: Mathlib `gramSchmidtNormed`/`gramSchmidtOrthonormalBasis` is the classical form on an inner product space; the matrix statement and the MGS recursion are the targets. Same pattern as `IsGradedKrylovBasis`. The matrix recursion is identified with Mathlib gramSchmidtNormed by the normalized rank-one projection identity. No linear independence is added to the bridge; dependent and zero columns follow the total normalization convention.

results.title: Householder reflector: symmetric, orthogonal, involutive, maps x to ∓‖x‖e₁
results.informal: $H_v = I - 2 v v^\top / (v^\top v)$ for $v \ne 0$ ($H_0 = I$): $H_v^\top = H_v$, $H_v^2 = I$, $H_v v = -v$, $H_v$ fixes $v^\perp$. With $v = x + \operatorname{sign}(x_1)\|x\| e_1$, $H_v x = -\operatorname{sign}(x_1)\|x\| e_1$. Here $\operatorname{sign}(t)$ means $+1$ at $t\ge0$ and $-1$ at $t<0$, as in `householderSign`; in particular its value at zero is one.
results.conclusion: $H_v$ orthogonal symmetric involution; $H_v x = \mp \|x\| e_1$ for the standard choice of $v$

formalizations.usage: The **Householder reflector** `H_v = I − (2 / vᵀv) v vᵀ`.
`H_v` is symmetric.
`H_v` is an involution, `H_v² = I`.
`H_v` is orthogonal, `H_vᵀ H_v = I`.
`H_v` has orthonormal columns.
`H_v v = −v`.
`H_v` fixes the hyperplane `v^⊥`.
The sign used by Trefethen–Bau: `sign t = 1` for `t ≥ 0` and `−1` for `t < 0` (so `sign 0 = 1`).
The **Trefethen–Bau Householder vector** `v = x + sign(x_{i₀}) ‖x‖ e_{i₀}`, whose reflector maps `x` to `−sign(x_{i₀}) ‖x‖ e_{i₀}` (`householder_mulVec_householderVector`).
**The reflector maps `x` onto the axis**: `H_v x = −sign(x_{i₀}) ‖x‖ e_{i₀}` for the Trefethen–Bau vector `v = householderVector x i₀`.

results.notes: Sign convention as in T&B (avoid cancellation); both signs are valid reflectors.

results.title: Householder QR: every A = QR with Q a product of n reflectors
results.informal: The Householder recursion (reflect column $k$ of the current matrix below the diagonal to zero) is total, needs no rank hypothesis, and returns reflectors $H_1,\dots,H_n$ and upper triangular $R$ with $H_n \cdots H_1 A = R$, i.e. $A = QR$ with $Q = H_1 \cdots H_n$ orthogonal (full QR); the first $n$ columns of $Q$ give the thin QR.
hypotheses: $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, $m \ge n$ (or any $m$ with the obvious truncation)
results.conclusion: $A = QR$, $Q$ orthogonal as a product of reflectors, $R$ upper triangular

formalizations.usage: **Householder QR** as a total recursion (Trefethen–Bau Alg.
The orthogonal factor of Householder QR: the product `H₁ H₂ ⋯ H_k` of the reflectors.
The triangular factor of Householder QR.
Apply `NLAlib.hasOrthonormalCols_householderQ` with its displayed hypotheses: The Householder `Q` is orthogonal (no hypothesis).
The Householder `R` is upper trapezoidal (no hypothesis).

**Realisation of Householder QR**: `(householderQ A, householderR A)` is a full QR of every real `m × n` matrix, with `Q` the product of `min m n` reflectors; no rank or shape hypothesis (unlike Gram–Schmidt).
**`QR = A` for Householder QR**, for every `A`.
**Thin QR from Householder** (`n ≤ m`): the first `n` columns of the Householder `Q` and the first `n` rows of `R`.

results.notes: Realisation theorem for `IsQR` (full form) with no hypothesis, unlike Gram–Schmidt.

results.title: Givens rotations and QR of Hessenberg and tridiagonal matrices
results.informal: A Givens rotation $G(i,j,\theta)$ is the identity except for the $2\times2$ rotation block in rows/columns $i,j$; it is orthogonal and can zero one chosen entry. An upper Hessenberg $H$ has $H = QR$ with $Q$ a product of $n-1$ rotations; $RQ$ is again upper Hessenberg (tridiagonal if $H$ is symmetric tridiagonal).
results.conclusion: $G$ orthogonal; $G x$ zeroes $x_j$; Hessenberg QR in $n-1$ rotations; $RQ$ Hessenberg

formalizations.usage: The **Givens rotation** in the `(i, j)` plane with cosine `c` and sine `s`: row `i` is `c eᵢᵀ + s eⱼᵀ`, row `j` is `−s eᵢᵀ + c eⱼᵀ`, every other row is that of the identity.

Apply `NLAlib.hasOrthonormalCols_givens` with the actual Givens recursion step to obtain its column-support invariant and resulting Hessenberg preservation (see its indexed signature for this component's exact hypotheses).
The cosine of the rotation zeroing `b` against `a`: `a / √(a² + b²)`, and `1` when `a = b = 0` (so that the rotation is always orthogonal).
The sine of the rotation zeroing `b` against `a`: `b / √(a² + b²)` (`0` when `a = b = 0`).
The rotation in the `(i, j)` plane that zeroes `x_j` against `x_i`.

Apply `NLAlib.givensRotation_transpose_mulVec_apply_right` with the actual Givens recursion step to obtain its column-support invariant and resulting Hessenberg preservation (see its indexed signature for this component's exact hypotheses).

Apply `NLAlib.givensRotation_transpose_mulVec_apply_left` with the actual Givens recursion step to obtain its column-support invariant and resulting Hessenberg preservation (see its indexed signature for this component's exact hypotheses).
**`RQ` of a Hessenberg matrix is Hessenberg**: if `H` is upper Hessenberg and `H = QR` is a QR factorization with `R` invertible, then `RQ` is upper Hessenberg.
**`RQ` of a symmetric tridiagonal matrix is symmetric tridiagonal** (for a QR with invertible `R`).
The matrix after `k` rotations: `H₀ = H`, `H_{k+1} = G_k H_k`.
The accumulated orthogonal factor after `k` rotations: `Q₀ = I`, `Q_{k+1} = Q_k G_kᵀ`, i.e.
**Hessenberg QR by Givens rotations**: `(Q, R) = (G_0ᵀ ⋯ G_{n−2}ᵀ, G_{n−2} ⋯ G_0 H)`, using `n − 1` rotations.
**The Givens recursion triangularises an upper Hessenberg matrix**: `G_{n−2} ⋯ G_0 H` is upper triangular.

results.title: Monic orthogonal polynomials of a measure on ℝ: existence, uniqueness, finite case
results.informal: For a finite positive Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R$ with finite moments, $(p,q)_\mu=\int pq\,d\mu$ is positive definite on $\mathcal P_n$ iff $\mu$ has at least $n+1$ support points; then Gram–Schmidt on $1,t,\dots,t^n$ gives the unique monic $\pi_0,\dots,\pi_n$ with $\deg\pi_k=k$ and $(\pi_k,\pi_l)_\mu=0$ ($k\ne l$), $\|\pi_k\|_\mu>0$. If $\mu$ has exactly $N$ support points there are exactly $N$ of them and the Gram–Schmidt $\pi_N$ is the node polynomial (norm $0$). For $\mu=\mu_b$ they are $\det(xI-T_k)$.
hypotheses: $\mu$ a finite positive measure on $\mathbb R$ with $\int|t|^k\,d\mu<\infty$ for all $k$ (e.g. compact support)
$n\in\mathbb N$ with $\#\operatorname{supp}\mu\ge n+1$
results.conclusion: There exist unique monic $\pi_0,\dots,\pi_n\in\mathbb R[X]$, $\deg\pi_k=k$, $\int\pi_k\pi_l\,d\mu=0$ for $k\ne l$ and $\int\pi_k^2\,d\mu>0$; any $p$ with $\deg p\le n$ orthogonal to all of them is $0$; for $\#\operatorname{supp}\mu=N$ the inner product is not positive definite on $\mathcal P_N$; for $\mu=\mu_b$, $\pi_k=\det(xI-T_k)$ for $k\le\operatorname{grade}(A,b)$.

results.title: Hankel moment matrices: positivity criterion and determinantal formulas
results.informal: With $M_n=[\mu_{i+j}]_{i,j<n}$ and $\Delta_n=\det M_n$: $(\cdot,\cdot)_\mu$ is positive definite on $\mathcal P_{n-1}$ iff $M_n\succ0$ iff $\Delta_1,\dots,\Delta_n>0$. For $\mu_b$, $M_n=K_n^\top K_n$ with $K_n=[b,Ab,\dots,A^{n-1}b]$, so $M_n\succ0$ iff $n\le\operatorname{grade}(A,b)$. Moreover $\pi_k$ is $\Delta_k^{-1}$ times the Hankel determinant with last row $(1,t,\dots,t^k)$, $\alpha_k=\Delta'_{k+1}/\Delta_{k+1}-\Delta'_k/\Delta_k$, $\beta_k=\Delta_{k+1}\Delta_{k-1}/\Delta_k^2$.
hypotheses: $\mu$ is a positive measure with the stated finite absolute polynomial moments; $L(p)=\int p\,d\mu$, $M_n=[L(t^{i+j})]_{i,j<n}$ and $\Delta_n=\det M_n$, with $\Delta_0=1$.
$E_0=0$; for $k\ge1$, $E_k$ is the determinant with rows $0,\ldots,k-1$ and columns $0,\ldots,k-2,k$ of the Hankel moment array. This is the precise shifted determinant denoted $\Delta_k^\prime$.

Use the monic polynomial determinant formula when $\Delta_k\ne0$, the alpha quotient when $h_k\ne0$, and the beta determinant ratio only at $k>0$ with nonzero denominator $\Delta_k$. The terminal beta may be zero; no normalized terminal polynomial or terminal alpha is asserted.
results.conclusion: $\int p^2\,d\mu=c^\top M_{d+1}c$ for $p=\sum c_kt^k$; positive definiteness on $\mathcal P_d$ iff $\Delta_1,\dots,\Delta_{d+1}>0$; determinantal formulas for $\pi_k$, $\alpha_k$, $\beta_k$; $M_n(\mu_b)=K_n^\top K_n$.

results.title: Jacobi eigenvectors, Christoffel numbers and discrete orthogonality
results.informal: For $\mu_b$ and $q\le\nu$ with orthonormal Lanczos polynomials $p_0,\dots,p_{q-1}$: $T_q\,\mathbf p(\theta_i)=\theta_i\,\mathbf p(\theta_i)$ with $\mathbf p=(p_0,\dots,p_{q-1})^\top$, so $u_i=\pm\mathbf p(\theta_i)/\|\mathbf p(\theta_i)\|$ and the Gauss weight is $\|b\|^2(e_1^\top u_i)^2=1/\sum_{k<q}p_k(\theta_i)^2$; the first $q$ orthonormal polynomials are orthonormal for the Gauss rule: $\sum_iw_ip_k(\theta_i)p_l(\theta_i)=\delta_{kl}$.
hypotheses: $A$ symmetric, $\mu_b=\sum_i (u_i^\top b)^2\delta_{\lambda_i}$ the spectral measure of symmetric $A$ and $b$ (`NLAlib.spectralMeasure`)
Lanczos decomposition of size $q\le\operatorname{grade}(A,b)$ with eigenpairs $(\theta_i,u_i)$ of $T_q$
results.conclusion: $T_q\mathbf p(\theta_i)=\theta_i\mathbf p(\theta_i)$; $w_i=\|b\|^2(e_1^\top u_i)^2=\big(\sum_{k<q}p_k(\theta_i)^2\big)^{-1}$; $\sum_iw_ip_k(\theta_i)p_l(\theta_i)=\delta_{kl}$ for $k,l<q$.
results.notes: Eigenvalue half of Thm 1.31 is in NLAlib (`integral_eval_charpoly_mul_eq_zero`); this adds the eigenvector and weight formulas. Consumers: `orthogonal-polynomial-zeros` (positive weights), `gauss-radau-lobatto`, SLQ weight analysis, Ritz-vector first components in Lanczos-FA error formulas. Prove (difficulty 2: evaluate `X_mul_poly` at a zero of $\det(xI-T_q)$).

results.title: Gauss quadrature remainder in derivative form (Markov); sign-definite Lanczos quadrature errors
results.informal: The $n$-point Gauss sum equals $\int H_{2n-1}f\,d\mu$, the integral of the Hermite interpolant of $f,f'$ at the nodes; hence for $f\in C^{2n}[a,b]$ ($[a,b]\supseteq\operatorname{supp}\mu$), $\int f\,d\mu-\sum\lambda_\nu f(\tau_\nu)=\frac{f^{(2n)}(\xi)}{(2n)!}\int\pi_n^2\,d\mu$. Matrix form: $b^\top f(A)b-\|b\|^2e_1^\top f(T_q)e_1=\frac{f^{(2q)}(\xi)}{(2q)!}\|\chi_q(A)b\|^2$ with $\chi_q=\det(xI-T_q)$, so the Lanczos value is a lower bound whenever $f^{(2q)}\ge0$ on the spectral interval (e.g. $f=1/x,\,x^{-2}$ on $(0,\infty)$; an upper bound for $\log$).
hypotheses: $A$ symmetric with spectrum in $[a,c]$, $\mu_b=\sum_i (u_i^\top b)^2\delta_{\lambda_i}$ the spectral measure of symmetric $A$ and $b$ (`NLAlib.spectralMeasure`)
Lanczos decomposition of size $q\le\operatorname{grade}(A,b)$, $T_q$, $\chi_q=\det(xI-T_q)$
$f\in C^{2q}[a,c]$
$a<c$ and positive quadrature order for an interior derivative witness.
results.conclusion: $\exists\xi\in(a,c)$: $b^\top f(A)b-\|b\|^2e_1^\top f(T_q)e_1=\frac{f^{(2q)}(\xi)}{(2q)!}\int\chi_q^2\,d\mu_b$; Gauss sum $=\int H_{2q-1}f\,d\mu_b$.

results.title: Gauss–Radau and Gauss–Lobatto rules via bordered Jacobi matrices; two-sided bounds for bᵀf(A)b
results.informal: Radau: bordering $T_q$ by $\beta_qe_q$ with corner $\alpha^R=a-\beta_q^2\chi_{q-1}(a)/\chi_q(a)$ gives $\hat T_{q+1}$ with eigenvalue $a$ whose Golub–Welsch rule is exact to degree $2q$ and has remainder $\frac{f^{(2q+1)}(\xi)}{(2q+1)!}\int(t-a)\chi_q^2(\cdot;\mu_b^a)\,d\mu_b$; so if $f^{(2q+1)}$ has constant sign on $[a,c]$ the Radau values at $a$ and at $c$ bracket $b^\top f(A)b$. Lobatto: a bordered $(q+2)\times(q+2)$ matrix with eigenvalues $a,c$ (corner and coupling from a $2\times2$ system) is exact to degree $2q+1$ with remainder of sign $-\operatorname{sgn}f^{(2q+2)}$. Applications: two-sided bounds for $\|x-x_k\|_2^2=r^\top A^{-2}r$, $\|x-x_k\|_A^2=r^\top A^{-1}r$ and $(A^{-1})_{ii}$; Lobatto discrete orthogonality (Thm 1.23); the Chebyshev Gauss–Lobatto rule (Ex 1.50). Here $\chi_q(t)=\det(tI-T_q)$ is monic, and the symmetric Jacobi off-diagonal is $\beta_q$ (the monic recurrence coefficient is its square).
hypotheses: $A$ real symmetric with spectrum in a strict interval $[a,c]$; $\mu_b$ is its original, unnormalized positive spectral measure.

Radau: the order-$q$ endpoint-shifted Gram matrix is positive definite and the prescribed endpoint is exterior to the $q$-node Jacobi spectrum; $q+1\le\operatorname{grade}(A,b)$ is a sufficient nondegenerate condition.

Lobatto: both $aI-T_{q+1}$ and $cI-T_{q+1}$ have the required strict exterior signs, so the derived coupling is positive; $q+2\le\operatorname{grade}(A,b)$ is sufficient. A shared $q+1\le\operatorname{grade}$ condition is not sufficient for positive Lobatto weights.

$f$ has the stated derivative regularity through order $2q+1$ for Radau and $2q+2$ for Lobatto. At exact support termination use the terminal Gauss rule; zero order and zero/singleton support have separate exact formulas.
results.conclusion: Radau and Lobatto rules from the bordered matrices are exact to degrees $2q$, $2q+1$; remainders have the stated derivative forms; for $f^{(2q+1)}>0$ (resp. $f^{(2q+2)}>0$) on $[a,c]$ the left Radau value is a lower bound, the right Radau an upper bound, and Lobatto an upper bound (signs flip with the derivative).

results.title: Kernel polynomials: orthogonal polynomials of (t−z)dμ, the qd/LR step on the Jacobi matrix, and the CG direction polynomials
results.informal: For a positive or quasi-definite polynomial functional $L$, suppose the required finite Hankel systems and original evaluations $\pi_j(z)$ are nonzero through the stated order. Then $\widehat\pi_j(t)=(\pi_{j+1}(t)+q_j\pi_j(t))/(t-z)$, with $q_j=-\pi_{j+1}(z)/\pi_j(z)$, is the canonical monic polynomial for $\widehat L(p)=L((t-z)p)$, and $\widehat h_j=q_jh_j$. Writing $e_j=\beta_{j+1}/q_j$, $\alpha_j=z+q_j+e_{j-1}$, $\widehat\alpha_j=z+q_j+e_j$, and $\widehat\beta_j=q_je_{j-1}$ for $j>0$, with the preceding term omitted at zero. The finite monic matrices satisfy $J_n-zI=L_nU_n$ and $\widehat J_n=U_nL_n+zI+e_{n-1}E_{n-1,n-1}$ for $n>0$; dimension zero is empty. For positive real measures, exterior real shifts derive denominator nonvanishing and transformed nonvanishing; arbitrary complex transformed nonvanishing is false. For SPD $A$ at $z=0$, the actual kernel Krylov vectors are the unique graded $A$-conjugate directions up to nonzero normalization, and the actual symmetric Lanczos matrix has its positive-pivot bidiagonal $LDL^\top$ factorization.
hypotheses: A positive measure with polynomial moments, or a bilinear polynomial functional with the finite nonsingular orthogonality systems actually used. Finite spectral measures require only the finite-prefix hypotheses, not global quasi-definiteness.
$\pi_j(z)\ne0$ through the required finite prefix, including the succeeding degree. For positive real measures and real $z$ outside a support enclosure, these evaluation conditions are derived.
Monic Jacobi off-diagonals are the norm ratios $\beta_j$; symmetric Jacobi off-diagonals are their square roots (or the signed coefficients of an actual Lanczos basis).

The SPD direction and symmetric LDL conclusions apply before the vector-relative Krylov termination threshold. Procedural CG normalization and coefficient recovery are separate algorithmic obligations.
results.conclusion: The actual finite Christoffel polynomial, norm, recurrence, forward LU and boundary-corrected reversed UL identities hold, including empty and finite-support terminal systems. Actual SPD spectral directions are nonzero and graded A-conjugate up to scalar normalization; actual symmetric Jacobi/Lanczos LDL pivots are positive.
results.notes: The uncorrected UL identity is valid for the infinite recurrence or a leading block taken from a larger product, not for equal-size finite factors. The mathematical CG direction interpretation is up to nonzero normalization; this card does not certify the separate procedural CG recursion.

Nonvanishing original evaluations make the required modified Hankel systems nonsingular; a globally quasi-definite functional remains quasi-definite under the all-order condition.

The quotient is the scaled reproducing kernel. At real modification points for a positive measure its transformed value is nonzero when the original value is nonzero; exterior real support intervals derive the original nonvanishing. No arbitrary complex transformed nonvanishing is asserted.

The original alpha coefficient equals z+q_n+e_(n-1) with zero boundary; modified alpha equals z+q_n+e_n and modified positive-order beta equals q_n e_(n-1), under only the required finite moment systems and nonvanishing evaluations. The alpha identity includes zero next norm at finite-support termination.

The actual finite monic Jacobi matrix minus zI equals its bidiagonal LU product, and the modified matrix equals the reversed product plus zI and its precise terminal-coordinate correction. Both hold under finite-prefix hypotheses and include empty and terminal atomic matrices.

The actual X-weighted spectral moment pairing is matrix A-energy; for SPD A it is nondegenerate through grade and derives zero-shift denominator nonvanishing. The actual finite spectral and energy-weighted monic Jacobi matrices have their respective forward and corrected reversed Christoffel factorization.

Before termination the actual zero-shift Christoffel Krylov vectors are nonzero graded directions and mutually A-conjugate. Every nonzero direction in the next Krylov space orthogonal in A-energy to the preceding space is their nonzero scalar multiple, establishing the mathematical CG direction interpretation up to normalization.

For an actual SPD symmetric Jacobi matrix the recursively defined LDL pivots are positive and the explicit unit lower bidiagonal LDL transpose product equals the matrix. The actual SPD Lanczos compression has the same positive-pivot factorization.

results.title: Quasi-definite measures and formal orthogonal polynomials
results.informal: A real or complex measure (moment functional) is quasi-definite if all Hankel determinants are nonzero; then and only then there is a unique sequence of monic formal orthogonal polynomials, and they satisfy a three-term recurrence with $\beta_k\ne0$ for $k\ge1$ (the recurrence boundary coefficient at zero is zero).
hypotheses: a linear functional $L$ on $\mathbb C[X]$ (moments $\mu_r=L(t^r)$)
results.conclusion: monic formal orthogonal polynomials exist and are unique iff $\Delta_n\ne0$ for all $n$; they satisfy $\pi_{k+1}=(t-\alpha_k)\pi_k-\beta_k\pi_{k-1}$ with $\beta_k\ne0$ for $k\ge1$.
results.notes: Consumer: two-sided (nonsymmetric) Lanczos and BiCG breakdown theory (no atlas entry yet). Prove.

results.title: Monic recurrence for det(xI − T_j), norm products, monic and confluent Christoffel–Darboux
results.informal: Write $\chi_j(x)=\det(xI-T_j)$, $\chi_0=1$, $h_j=\int\chi_j^2\,d\mu_b$, and $h_0=\|b\|^2$. The signed stored Lanczos coupling is $a_j=T_{j,j-1}$ (Lean D.beta), whereas the monic recurrence coefficient is $\beta_j=h_j/h_{j-1}=a_j^2$ for $0<j<q$; $\beta_0=0$ is a recurrence boundary, not the mass. For $j+1\le q$, $\chi_{j+1}=(x-\alpha_j)\chi_j-\beta_j\chi_{j-1}$, with the preceding term omitted at $j=0$. For $j<q$, $h_j=h_0\prod_{i=1}^j a_i^2$ and $\alpha_j=\int t\chi_j^2\,d\mu_b/h_j$. In the generic monic recurrence $h_j=h_0\prod_{i=1}^j\beta_i$, including exact support termination $h_N=\beta_N=0$. A nonterminal order-$q$ norm product needs the next actual coupling; the totalized size-$q$ value D.beta q is zero and cannot supply it. Monic Christoffel–Darboux is $(x-y)\sum_{k\le n}(\prod_{i=k+1}^{n}\beta_i)\chi_k(x)\chi_k(y)=\chi_{n+1}(x)\chi_n(y)-\chi_n(x)\chi_{n+1}(y)$. Its norm-divided confluent form is $\sum_{k<m}\chi_k(x)^2/h_k=(\chi_m^{\prime}(x)\chi_{m-1}(x)-\chi_{m-1}^{\prime}(x)\chi_m(x))/h_{m-1}>0$, requiring $m>0$ and only the preceding positive norms. If $h_m>0$, the normalized kernel can also be written with coefficient $\sqrt{\beta_m}$; actual signed Lanczos polynomials use their signed $a_m$ and $1\le m<q$. The actual continued-fraction denominator continuants equal $\chi_j$ for every leading order $j\le q$, including zero and exact grade.
hypotheses: $A$ is real symmetric and $\mu_b=\sum_i(u_i^\top b)^2\delta_{\lambda_i}$ is its original spectral measure, of mass $\|b\|^2$. The actual Lanczos decomposition has size $q\le\operatorname{grade}(A,b)$.

Signed Lanczos couplings a_j are stored only for 0<j<q. The monic coefficient β_j is the norm ratio, equal to a_j² on these stored indices; β_0=0 is distinct from h_0. The monic alpha quotient is used only where h_j>0, in particular j<q; no terminal zero-norm alpha is asserted.

The actual characteristic recurrence includes j+1≤q, including the final polynomial, and uses only the preceding stored coupling. Norm products using size-q stored couplings require j<q. At a nonterminal top order use a larger decomposition or the next actual coupling; at exact grade the final monic norm and terminal beta are zero.

The monic multiplied Christoffel–Darboux identity holds for all x,y, with the needed finite nonsingular Hankel systems. Its divided form requires x≠y. Positive confluent kernels require m>0 and h_0,…,h_(m−1)>0 and may use a zero-norm terminal top monic polynomial. The fully normalized top-polynomial form additionally requires h_m>0; the actual signed size-q formula uses 1≤m<q.

Characteristic/continuant identification includes every leading order j≤q and does not require literal nested fraction denominators to be nonzero. Evaluating an ordinary nested fraction uses the denominator conditions of jacobi-matrix-identities.
results.conclusion: The actual leading characteristic polynomials have the monic three-term recurrence, stored-index norm products and alpha/beta norm quotients; generic finite monic norm products, terminal zero norms, monic and normalized confluent kernels, and actual continued-fraction denominator identification hold with the stated boundary conventions.
